The road to exam day

Six phases take you from “I don’t know what a mole is” to walking out of your last paper. Each phase has its own page with exactly what to do, for how long, and how to know you are ready to move on.

  1. Fix your foundationsCheck the GCSE/IGCSE skills every A Level assumes.
  2. Learn the contentWork through each chapter here, one topic at a time.
  3. PractiseTest yourself until you can do it without notes.
  4. Past papersTimed papers, mark schemes and an error log.
  5. Final revisionThe last eight weeks, planned day by day.
  6. Exam dayThe night before, the paper itself, results and resits.

Choose a subject

The six main subjects are taught in full, from absolute basics to the hardest A Level ideas. The code on each card is the Cambridge International syllabus number. Each chapter also notes where Pearson Edexcel, AQA and OCR differ.

How this guide works

Every chapter is written for someone meeting the topic for the first time. It starts with the idea in plain English, builds up step by step, and finishes at real exam standard. Look out for these parts:

AaKey term cards hold the exact definitions examiners expect. They are also collected in the glossary.
M1Worked examples show every step, with marks: M for method, A for an accurate answer, B for an independent fact.
✗Common mistakes are the errors examiners see every year, and how to avoid them.
!Exam technique notes explain what the question really wants and where the marks are.
≠Board differences say where Edexcel, AQA or OCR do things differently from Cambridge.
✓Try it yourself questions have full answers, and Quick checks mark you instantly. Tick Mark as learned to track progress.

Tools you can use any time

What are A Levels?

Start hereStudy time20 minutes

A Levels are two-year qualifications in single subjects, usually taken at 16–18 after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level, and used for university entry around the world. This chapter explains how they work, how they compare with other systems, and what studying them is really like.

Why this matters

Before you open a textbook, it helps to know the rules of the game. Students lose time and money because nobody explained the basics: which exam board they are entered for, whether their first-year exams count, or which subjects their chosen degree requires. The next twenty minutes will save you months later.

A Levels in plain English

A Level is short for Advanced Level. An A Level is a qualification in one subject, such as Mathematics, Chemistry or Business. Most students study three of them at the same time, over two years, between the ages of 16 and 18. At the end you receive one grade for each subject, from A* (the highest) down to E.

A Level

An Advanced Level qualification in a single subject, normally studied over two years after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level and graded A* to E. It is the main qualification for university entry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and schools in many other countries offer it too.

A Levels follow the exams most students take at about 16: GCSE (General Certificate of Secondary Education) in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, IGCSE (International GCSE) in international schools, or O Level (Ordinary Level), still offered by Cambridge in some countries.

In England, the two A Level years are Year 12 and Year 13, together called the sixth form. In Turkey they match the ages of Grades 11 and 12 of lise. Scotland has its own system (Highers and Advanced Highers), so A Levels are less common there.

Two halves: AS and A2

An A Level course splits naturally into two halves of about one year each.

AS Level

Advanced Subsidiary Level: a qualification covering roughly the first half of an A Level, normally studied in one year. Cambridge International grades it a to e (lower-case letters); UK boards use A to E. There is no A* at AS Level.

The second half is usually called A2, and this guide labels first-year content “AS” and second-year content “A2”.

Whether your AS result counts depends on the exam board:

Exam board Does the AS count towards the full A Level?
Cambridge International Yes, on the “staged” route: AS first, then the result is carried forward. You can also sit everything at the end.
Pearson Edexcel International (IAL) Yes: the first-year units make up half the qualification.
AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas in England No. The AS is a separate qualification; all A Level exams come at the end of Year 13.
WJEC (Wales) and CCEA (Northern Ireland) Yes. The AS is worth 40% of the A Level.

How many subjects, and which grades?

Most students take three A Levels. Students who choose Further Mathematics usually take four, because Further Maths is studied alongside Mathematics, not instead of it. Some schools ask everyone to start four subjects and drop one at the end of the first year, keeping it as an AS.

Qualification Pass grades, highest first
A Level (all boards) A*, A, B, C, D, E
AS Level (Cambridge International) a, b, c, d, e
AS Level (UK boards) A, B, C, D, E

A result below E is recorded as U (ungraded), which is not a pass. Universities usually make offers in grades, such as “AAB”, or in UCAS tariff points, which turn grades into numbers. Grades, marks and UCAS points explains both.

How much work is an A Level?

Guided learning hours

The time a student spends being taught, or doing study directed and supervised by a teacher, for a qualification. Cambridge International plans for about 360 guided learning hours for each A Level and about 180 for each AS Level. Private study comes on top.

Two school years have about 36 teaching weeks each, so 360 hours works out at about 5 hours of teaching per subject per week. Add homework, revision and practice, and a normal A Level week looks like this:

Activity Hours per subject per week For three subjects
Lessons (or, if you study alone, working through chapters) 4–5 12–15
Homework and reviewing notes 2–3 6–9
Practice questions, and later past papers 1–2 3–6
Total 7–10 21–30

Three A Levels are close to a full-time job. In school, that means lessons in each subject on most days, homework in every subject, and a short test or practical most weeks. If you study alone, you are teacher and student at once: lesson time becomes reading, working through examples and checking answers.

TipA self-study week that works

Give each subject at least three separate sessions a week rather than one long one: short, regular sessions beat a weekend marathon because you forget less in between. Keep one session a week for older topics. Build your personal study plan turns your exam date into a week-by-week timetable.

Why depth matters

At IGCSE you probably studied eight to ten subjects. At A Level you study three, and each goes much deeper: A Level Chemistry, for example, explains why reactions happen and asks you to predict ones you have never seen.

Because of this depth, examiners test understanding more than memory. Only part of the marks are for recalling facts; the rest reward applying ideas to unfamiliar situations, handling data, and analysing or evaluating.

Assessment objectives (AOs)

The skills an exam is designed to reward, listed with their weightings in every syllabus. Typical AOs are knowledge and understanding, application, and analysis and evaluation; science subjects also have one for experimental skills.

Think of it like this

IGCSE checks that you can follow a recipe. A Level checks whether you can cook a good meal from whatever is in the fridge. You still need to know the recipes, but the marks go to people who understand why each step works.

Most students find the first term the hardest: the pace is faster, the ideas are more abstract, and you are expected to work more independently. This is normal, and it is why every chapter in this guide starts from zero and builds up in small steps. The same depth is why universities value A Levels: two years of serious work on a few hard subjects is excellent preparation for a degree.

Who uses A Levels?

A Levels are the standard entry qualification for UK universities, and universities in many other countries accept them too. Each university sets its own requirements, so always check the entry requirements for international students on each course page.

Several organisations, called exam boards, write and mark A Levels. Schools in the UK use boards such as AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel, WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA. International schools mostly use Cambridge International (often shortened to CAIE) or Pearson Edexcel International (IAL), and OxfordAQA also offers international A Levels. UK universities accept A Levels from all the major boards. This guide follows Cambridge International and points out where the others differ.

How A Levels compare with other systems

A Levels IB Diploma US Advanced Placement (AP) National systems (e.g. Turkey)
Length 2 years 2 years Usually 1 year per course Final years of school, then an entrance exam
Subjects Usually 3, in depth 6 (3 Higher Level, 3 Standard Level) plus a core Any number of single-subject exams A broad school curriculum
Extra parts Optional Extended Project (EPQ) at UK boards Theory of Knowledge, Extended Essay, CAS None Varies by country
Grading A* to E per subject 1 to 7 per subject, 45 points maximum 1 to 5 per exam School grades plus an exam score
Main use University entry in the UK and worldwide University entry worldwide US college admission and credit Entry to that country’s universities

None of these is “better”. The IB Diploma suits students who want breadth (CAS stands for creativity, activity, service). AP exams are taken alongside an American high school diploma, and UK universities usually ask for several AP scores as well as the diploma. National systems, such as Turkey’s lise diploma plus the YKS entrance exam run by ÖSYM, are designed mainly for entry to that country’s own universities. A Levels suit students who are ready to specialise.

NoteStudying in Turkey?

A Levels do not replace the YKS for most places at Turkish universities. Students in Turkey usually take A Levels to apply abroad, and many UK universities ask applicants from Turkey for A Levels, the IB, AP results or a foundation year rather than the national diploma alone. To keep both routes open, check the current rules with ÖSYM and with each university.

Can anyone take A Levels?

Yes. There is no age limit, and you do not need to be at a school. Adults, home-schooled students and school students adding a subject their school does not teach can all enter as a private candidate.

Private candidate

A student who enters for exams through an approved exam centre without being taught there. Private candidates sit the same papers and receive the same grades and certificates as school students.

Private candidates register with an exam centre that accepts external students, pay the fees and sit the exams there. In Turkey, the British Council (in Istanbul and Ankara) and some approved schools act as centres. Sciences need care: Cambridge’s science A Levels include a laboratory exam that your centre must be able to run, while Edexcel International tests practical skills in written papers, one reason many private candidates choose it. Studying as a private candidate explains the process.

Where to go from here

  1. Decide roughly what, and where, you want to study next.
  2. Check the subjects that degree needs: Choosing your subjects.
  3. Pick a board and exam series: Exam boards and how the exams work.
  4. Learn how grades and offers work: Grades, marks and UCAS points.
  5. Make a plan and start: How to use this guide.
Quick check
Summary
  • An A Level is a two-year qualification in one subject, usually taken at 16–18 after GCSE, IGCSE or O Level.
  • Most students take three A Levels, or four if they add Further Mathematics.
  • A Level grades are A* to E. AS grades are a to e (Cambridge) or A to E (UK boards), with no A* at AS.
  • The AS counts towards the A Level at Cambridge (if carried forward), Edexcel International, WJEC and CCEA, but not with the boards in England.
  • Each A Level is designed for about 360 guided learning hours (about 5 hours of teaching a week), plus your own study.
  • A Levels reward understanding and application, not just memory, and universities worldwide accept them.
  • Anyone can take A Levels at any age, including as a private candidate.

Exam boards and how the exams work

Start hereStudy time25 minutes

Who sets A Level exams, how Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel International and the boards in England organise them, when exams and results happen, and how papers, mark schemes and grade boundaries work.

Why this matters

Two students can both be “doing A Level Physics” and sit completely different exams: different papers, different months, different resit rules. Knowing your board and its rules tells you which syllabus to follow, which past papers to practise and when your deadlines fall.

What an exam board does

An exam board writes the syllabus, sets the papers, marks them and awards the grades. All boards teach broadly the same subjects at the same level, but the details differ: the exact topics, the number and style of papers, the exam months and the resit rules.

Exam board

An organisation that writes the syllabus for a qualification, sets and marks the exams, and awards grades and certificates. Also called an awarding body.

Syllabus

The official document listing exactly what can be examined in a subject, how the exams are structured and what each assessment objective is worth. Cambridge calls it a syllabus; Pearson and the UK boards call it a specification.

The main boards

Board Qualification Where it is used
Cambridge International (CAIE) Cambridge International AS & A Level International schools in many countries; private candidates at approved centres
Pearson Edexcel International International Advanced Level (IAL) International schools; widely used by private candidates, including at British Council centres
AQA AS and A Level Schools in England
OCR AS and A Level Schools in England
Pearson Edexcel (UK) AS and A Level Schools in England, and some British schools abroad
WJEC / Eduqas AS and A Level WJEC in Wales; Eduqas is the same organisation’s brand in England

Northern Ireland has its own board, CCEA, and OxfordAQA offers international A Levels in some countries. Cambridge International and OCR both belong to Cambridge University Press & Assessment, but they set different qualifications. AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas follow the same rules for A Levels in England, set by the regulator Ofqual, so their A Levels share one structure.

Cambridge International: AS first, or everything at the end

A Cambridge A Level is made of several papers, which Cambridge calls components. The AS papers make up the AS Level and also half of the full A Level; the A Level adds more papers on second-year content. You can take them in three ways:

  1. AS Level only. Sit the AS papers and receive an AS qualification.
  2. Staged route. Sit the AS papers in one series and the remaining A Level papers in a later one. Your AS result is carried forward and combined with them.
  3. Linear route. Sit every paper, AS and A Level, in the same series at the end of the course.

An AS result can be carried forward to complete the A Level within 13 months. In practice, an AS taken in June can be completed in the following June series.

Common mistakeThe 13-month rule

If you sit AS in June 2026, you must complete the A Level by the June 2027 series for the AS to count. If you wait longer, you would have to sit all the papers, AS ones included, in a single series.

A real example is Cambridge International AS & A Level Physics (9702). Chemistry (9701) and Biology (9700) follow the same pattern.

Paper Type Time Marks Share of A Level
1 Multiple choice (AS) 1 h 15 min 40 15.5%
2 AS structured questions 1 h 15 min 60 23%
3 Advanced practical skills (laboratory exam) 2 h 40 11.5%
4 A Level structured questions 2 h 100 38.5%
5 Planning, analysis and evaluation 1 h 15 min 30 11.5%

Papers 1–3 form the AS (50% of the A Level); Papers 4 and 5 are the second-year papers.

Cambridge runs two main exam series each year: June (exams from roughly late April to mid-June) and November (October and November). A third, March, series is available in India only. June results come out in August (the June 2026 A Level results were released on 11 August 2026), and November results in January.

Exam series

A period in which a board runs a full set of exams, named after its main month, such as the June series or the November series.

Pearson Edexcel International: units taken in stages

An IAL is modular: it is split into units, each examined by one paper. IAL sciences have six units, three for the International AS and three more for the full IAL. IAL Mathematics also has six: four Pure units and two applied units (mechanics, statistics or decision mathematics).

Modular qualification

A qualification split into separately examined units that can be taken at different times, with the results combined at the end. Edexcel International A Levels are modular; A Levels from the boards in England are linear.

  • There are three sittings a year: January, May/June and October/November. Most units are offered in every sitting.
  • You can spread units over several sittings, for example Pure 1 in January and Pure 2 in June.
  • You can resit a unit to improve it, and the better result counts.
  • Each unit’s raw mark is converted to a uniform mark so that units from different sittings can be added fairly (how this works).
  • When you have all the units you need, your centre claims the qualification (called “cashing in”) and your overall grade is calculated.
  • In the sciences, practical skills are tested in written papers (Units 3 and 6), not in a laboratory exam.

The boards in England: linear A Levels

A Levels from AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel and Eduqas are linear:

  • Every exam that counts is sat in May and June at the end of Year 13.
  • The AS is a separate qualification whose marks never count towards the A Level, so many schools no longer enter students for it.
  • There is one exam series a year, in the summer. To improve a grade, you resit all the exam papers the following summer; coursework marks can usually be carried forward.
  • In Biology, Chemistry and Physics you also receive a Practical Endorsement, reported separately as Pass or Not classified, based on at least 12 practical activities assessed by your teacher. Many universities expect a Pass.
  • Some subjects include coursework, officially called non-exam assessment (NEA): typically 20% in History, Geography, English Literature and Computer Science, and more in subjects such as Design and Technology and Art.

The three systems side by side

Cambridge International Edexcel International (IAL) Boards in England
Structure Papers; AS papers form half the A Level Units; AS units form half the IAL Linear: all papers at the end
Does the AS count? Yes, if carried forward within 13 months Yes No
Exam series June and November (March in India only) January, May/June, October/November Summer only
Improving a grade Retake in a later series Resit single units; the better result counts Resit all papers the next summer
Science practicals Laboratory exam plus a planning paper Written practical-skills papers Practical Endorsement plus practical questions in written papers
Results August (June series), January (November series) Roughly two months after each sitting Mid-August
Board differences

WJEC A Levels in Wales and CCEA A Levels in Northern Ireland are unitised: the AS counts for 40% of the A Level. Scotland uses its own qualifications (Highers and Advanced Highers). Rules change from time to time, so always check the current syllabus for your board.

What the papers look like

Paper type What you do Common in
Multiple choice Answer 30–40 questions, each with four options Cambridge sciences, Economics, Accounting
Structured questions Answer a question in parts (a), (b), (c): short answers, calculations, explanations Every subject
Extended response Write a long answer, marked by “levels of response” Business, Economics, English, History
Data response or case study Answer questions on unseen data, a text or a business case Business, Economics, Geography
Practical exam Carry out experiments in a laboratory under exam conditions Cambridge sciences
Planning and analysis Plan an experiment and analyse given results, on paper Cambridge and Edexcel International sciences
Coursework (NEA) Complete a project over several weeks, marked by teachers and checked by the board Some subjects at the boards in England

Mark schemes, examiner reports and grade boundaries

After each series, boards publish three documents that are gold for revision:

  • Mark schemes show exactly what earned each mark. In Maths they use M (method), A (accuracy) and B (independent) marks; in essay subjects they describe levels of response.
  • Examiner reports explain, question by question, what candidates did well and where they lost marks.
  • Grade boundaries (Cambridge calls them grade thresholds) give the minimum mark for each grade. They are set after marking, for each paper in each series. Grades, marks and UCAS points explains why they move.

Cambridge puts a selection of past papers, mark schemes and examiner reports on its public website, and schools get more through its School Support Hub. Pearson, AQA and OCR publish theirs on their qualification pages, although the most recent papers are sometimes released to teachers first.

Exam techniqueUse mark schemes from day one

Do not wait for “past-paper season”. After every topic, try two or three past-paper questions on it and mark them yourself with the official scheme. You will quickly learn which words and steps examiners need to see. Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes shows a full method.

Entries and deadlines

You cannot simply turn up on exam day. Your school, or your exam centre if you are a private candidate, must enter you for each paper months before the series. For a June series, the deadline usually falls early in the same year, and many centres set their own earlier deadline. Late entries, if accepted at all, cost extra. Fees are set by each centre and vary, so ask for the full price per subject, including any centre charges.

Common mistakeConfirm four things before you start studying

Check with your centre: the board, the syllabus code (for example 9702 for Cambridge Physics), the exam series, and the entry deadline. A year spent studying the wrong syllabus is an expensive mistake.

Quick check
Summary
  • An exam board writes the syllabus, sets and marks the papers and awards grades. Always study the syllabus with the correct code for your exam year.
  • Cambridge: papers called components; AS papers form half the A Level; take AS only, AS first (carried forward within 13 months), or everything at the end.
  • Cambridge series: June (results in August) and November (results in January); March in India only.
  • Edexcel International: modular units, sittings in January, May/June and October/November, single-unit resits, and written practical-skills papers.
  • Boards in England: linear, all exams in May–June of Year 13, AS does not count, Practical Endorsement in sciences, NEA in some subjects.
  • Mark schemes, examiner reports and grade boundaries are published after each series: use them throughout the course.
  • Entries close months before the exams, so confirm your board, syllabus code, series and deadline early.

Grades, marks and UCAS points

Start hereStudy time25 minutes

How raw marks become grades, why grade boundaries move, how the A* is awarded, and how UCAS tariff points, university offers and predicted grades work.

Why this matters

Your grades open university doors, so it pays to know exactly how they are calculated. Understanding grade boundaries also changes how you study: it shows why every single mark matters, and why a hard paper is not a disaster.

The grades

Qualification Pass grades, highest first
A Level A*, A, B, C, D, E
AS Level a, b, c, d, e at Cambridge; A, B, C, D, E at UK boards

A result below the lowest pass grade is reported as ungraded (U), and no qualification is awarded in that subject. Your certificate shows a grade for each subject, not a percentage.

From raw marks to a grade

Each paper is marked and you receive a raw mark. Your raw marks are combined, using each paper’s weighting, and the total is compared with the grade boundaries for that series.

Raw mark

The number of marks you actually score on a paper, before any conversion; for example, 52 out of 75.

Grade boundary

The minimum mark needed for a particular grade on a paper or qualification in a given exam series. Boundaries are set after marking and can change from series to series. Cambridge calls them grade thresholds.

Why boundaries move

No two papers are equally difficult. If this year’s paper is harder than last year’s, the same student scores fewer marks. To keep an A worth the same every year, senior examiners study the papers, samples of marked scripts and statistics, and then set the boundaries. A harder paper gets lower boundaries; an easier paper gets higher ones.

Mark needed (out of 100) Series 1: harder paper Series 2: easier paper
Grade A 68 76
Grade C 47 55

These numbers are invented to show the idea; each board publishes the real boundaries for every series. Three lessons follow:

  1. There is no fixed percentage for an A. “70% is an A” is a myth.
  2. A hard paper is hard for everyone. If a paper feels brutal, keep collecting marks: the boundaries will reflect it.
  3. Every mark counts. Neighbouring grades are often separated by only a handful of marks on each paper, so one extra method mark here and there can lift a whole grade.
TipEstimating your grade from a past paper

Mark the paper with the official mark scheme, then compare your total with the published boundaries for that same series, not this year’s or an average. Do this for papers from several different years to get a fair picture.

How the A* is awarded

  • Cambridge International awards A* for the full A Level only, based on your total across all the papers. There is no A* at AS.
  • Edexcel International requires an A overall plus an especially high score on the A2 (second-year) units, so an A* reflects strength in the hardest material.
  • The boards in England set the A* as the top boundary on your total mark, like any other grade.

Uniform marks at Edexcel International

In a modular system, you might sit one unit in a January with a hard paper and another in a June with an easy one. Simply adding the raw marks would be unfair. Pearson solves this with uniform marks.

Uniform mark

A raw unit mark converted onto a fixed scale, so that results from papers of different difficulty, taken in different sittings, can be added fairly. The grade boundaries on the uniform scale stay the same every series.

The conversion uses each sitting’s grade boundaries: a raw mark exactly on the A boundary always becomes the same uniform mark, however hard the paper was. Your uniform marks from all the units are then added, and the total decides your overall grade. Pearson’s results show the uniform mark for each unit, which tells you how close you were to the next grade.

Think of it like this

Uniform marks work like currency exchange. Raw marks from different sittings are like dollars, euros and lira: you cannot add them directly. Converting everything into one currency first lets you add them fairly.

UCAS tariff points

UCAS (the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service) handles applications to UK universities. Its tariff turns grades into points so that different qualifications can be compared.

UCAS tariff points

A points system that converts qualifications and grades into numbers so that different qualifications can be compared. Some universities state their entry requirements in tariff points.

Grade A Level AS Level Extended Project (EPQ)
A* 56 no A* 28
A (AS: a) 48 20 24
B (AS: b) 40 16 20
C (AS: c) 32 12 16
D (AS: d) 24 10 12
E (AS: e) 16 6 8

An EPQ is worth exactly half an A Level at every grade. An AS that you later complete as a full A Level in the same subject does not count separately: only the A Level counts.

Worked exampleAdding up tariff points

A student has A Levels in Mathematics (A*), Physics (A) and Chemistry (B), an AS in Further Mathematics (grade b) and an EPQ (grade A). How many UCAS tariff points does she have?

A Levels: 56+48+40=144

AS Further Mathematics, grade b: 16

EPQ, grade A: 24

Total: 144+16+24=184 points.

Try your own combination in the calculator: choose a grade for each qualification and watch the total change.

Common mistakePoints are not everything

AAA and AAB are both worth 144 points, but a course asking for "AAA including Mathematics" accepts neither. Most selective universities make offers in grades and name the subjects. Use points only when a course actually asks for them.

What offers look like

You apply through UCAS to up to five courses (four at most in medicine, dentistry or veterinary science). Each university replies with an offer or a rejection. Typical offers read like this:

  • “AAA”: three A grades, sometimes excluding certain subjects.
  • “AAA, including A in Mathematics and A in Physics”: grades plus named subjects, as for many engineering courses.
  • “ABB including Biology and Chemistry”: a common pattern for life sciences.
  • “112 UCAS points, including a C in Business”: a tariff offer, which BBC would meet (40+40+32=112).
  • “AAB, or ABB with an A in the EPQ”: some universities lower an offer for a strong EPQ.
Conditional offer

A university place that becomes yours only if you meet stated conditions, usually particular grades. An unconditional offer has no grade conditions, usually because you already have your results.

From your offers you choose one firm choice and, if you wish, one insurance choice with lower grades as a backup. On results day, the university confirms your place if you meet the conditions. If you miss both, Clearing matches students without a place to courses that still have vacancies. Some courses also set admissions tests or interviews; see University applications and admissions tests.

Key factsUCAS deadlines for 2027 entry
  • 15 October 2026: Oxford, Cambridge, and most courses in medicine, dentistry and veterinary science.
  • 13 January 2027: deadline for equal consideration for most other courses.

Predicted grades

Universities usually decide before your final exams, so they rely on predictions.

Predicted grades

The grades your teachers expect you to achieve, entered on your UCAS application. Universities make most offers on the basis of predicted grades, because final results arrive after most decisions are made.

Teachers predict from evidence: classwork, mock exams, AS results if you have them, and the progress you have shown. A prediction below a course’s typical offer usually means no offer, so the evidence you give your teachers matters. Private candidates still need predicted grades and a reference; a tutor, a former teacher or a school can provide them. Studying as a private candidate explains how.

Exam techniqueEarn your predictions

Do your mocks properly, under timed conditions, and keep a record of your past-paper scores. A strong AS result, on Cambridge’s staged route or at Edexcel International, is the most convincing evidence of all.

Quick check
Summary
  • A Level grades run A* to E, AS grades a to e (Cambridge) or A to E (UK boards); U is not a pass.
  • Raw marks are compared with grade boundaries set after marking. Harder papers get lower boundaries, so there is no fixed percentage for an A.
  • Cambridge awards A* for the full A Level only. Edexcel International requires an A overall plus a very high score on the A2 units.
  • Edexcel International converts raw unit marks into uniform marks so that units from different sittings add up fairly.
  • UCAS tariff: A* 56, A 48, B 40, C 32, D 24, E 16; AS a 20, b 16, c 12, d 10, e 6; EPQ A* 28 down to E 8.
  • Selective universities mostly make grade offers that name subjects; some use tariff points.
  • Offers are based on predicted grades, so mocks and past-paper scores matter. For 2027 entry, UCAS deadlines are 15 October 2026 and 13 January 2027.

Next: Choosing your subjects.

PreviousExam boards and how the exams workNextChoosing your subjects
Start Here/Welcome

Choosing your subjects

Start hereStudy time30 minutes

How to choose A Level subjects that fit the degree or career you want: typical requirements for popular courses, how many subjects to take, strong combinations, entry requirements, honest workload notes and the mistakes to avoid.

Why this matters

Your A Level subjects decide which degrees you can apply for. At most universities you cannot study medicine without Chemistry, or engineering without Mathematics. An evening of research now protects options you may want in two years’ time.

Work backwards from your goal

The safest way to choose is to start at the end:

  1. Write down two or three degree courses you might want to study, even if you are unsure.
  2. Look up each course’s subject requirements on the websites of a few universities you like.
  3. Choose subjects that satisfy all of them, so you keep every option open.
  4. Fill any remaining place with a subject you enjoy and can do well in.

University websites separate subjects that are required from those that are only preferred, and the difference matters.

Required subject

An A Level subject that a course insists on; without it, an application is normally rejected. Universities also list “preferred” or “recommended” subjects, which strengthen an application but are not compulsory.

Typical requirements for popular courses

If you want to study Usually required Recommended or useful Also note
Medicine Chemistry, and usually Biology Maths or Physics UCAT at most schools; interviews; apply by 15 October
Dentistry Chemistry and Biology Maths or Physics UCAT at most schools; interviews; apply by 15 October
Veterinary science Chemistry and Biology Maths or Physics Animal work experience expected; apply by 15 October
Engineering Maths, and usually Physics Further Maths, strongly recommended for top courses; Chemistry for chemical engineering ESAT at some universities (e.g. Cambridge, Imperial, Oxford)
Computer science Maths Further Maths; Physics or Computer Science The A Level of the same name is rarely required; TMUA at some universities
Mathematics or physics Maths (and Physics for physics) Further Maths, often expected at top universities Admissions tests at some universities
Economics Maths at most selective universities Further Maths for the most competitive courses The A Level of the same name is rarely required; TMUA at some universities
Business, management, accounting Usually none Maths, especially for finance and accounting A Level Business is not required
Law None in the UK Essay subjects such as History, English Literature or a language LNAT at several universities
Architecture Often none Art or Design; Maths or Physics A portfolio of creative work is usually required
Psychology Often none Biology or Maths; some courses want one science A psychology degree contains a lot of statistics
Natural sciences Two or more of Maths, Physics, Chemistry and Biology Maths for any physical science Requirements depend on which sciences you plan to take

These are typical UK requirements. Every university sets its own, they change from year to year, and universities in other countries have different rules, so confirm the details on each course page for your year of entry. University applications and admissions tests explains UCAT, LNAT, TMUA and ESAT.

How many subjects?

Three A Levels is the standard, and university offers are almost always based on three. A fourth makes sense mainly when it is Further Mathematics, or when you are strong enough to take it without your other grades suffering. A fourth A Level rarely earns you a lower offer, but a weaker grade in one of your main three can cost you a place.

TipThe “3 + 1” option

If you cannot decide between four subjects, start all four. At Cambridge or Edexcel International you can sit the AS in one of them at the end of the first year and stop there, keeping a useful extra qualification. An AS at the boards in England is also possible, but it is a separate exam and many schools no longer offer it.

Strong combinations and keeping doors open

Combination Keeps these doors open
Maths, Physics, Chemistry Engineering, physics, chemistry, natural sciences, computer science
Maths, Further Maths, Physics Engineering, mathematics, physics, computer science: the strongest choice for the most competitive courses
Biology, Chemistry, plus Maths or Physics Medicine, dentistry, veterinary science, pharmacy, biomedical sciences, and still some physical sciences
Biology, Chemistry, Psychology Medicine at universities that accept any third subject, psychology, life sciences
Maths, Economics, plus History or Further Maths Economics, finance, management, politics
English Literature, History, plus a language or Politics Law, history, politics, languages, journalism
Maths, Physics, Art Architecture, design engineering

If you are not sure yet what you want to study, choose subjects that keep the most doors open:

  • Mathematics is the subject most often required or preferred: engineering, physics, computer science, economics and many sciences ask for it, and it helps with the statistics in psychology and biology.
  • Chemistry opens medicine, dentistry, veterinary science, pharmacy, biochemistry and chemical engineering.
  • One essay subject keeps law, the humanities and the social sciences possible.
  • It is easier to move from sciences to a humanities degree than the other way round, because most humanities degrees do not require particular subjects.

Entry requirements: are you ready?

Exam boards set no formal entry requirements, but schools do, and so does common sense: A Level builds directly on IGCSE. Typical school requirements look like this:

A Level subject Typical GCSE/IGCSE grade needed
Mathematics 7 (A), sometimes 6 (B)
Further Mathematics 8 or 9 (A*), and a confident start in A Level Maths
Physics, Chemistry, Biology 6 or 7 (B or A) in that science, and at least 6 in Maths
Essay subjects (History, English Literature) 6 (B) in English and a related subject
New subjects (Economics, Psychology, Law) Good grades in English and Maths; no earlier study needed

If you are teaching yourself and never took the IGCSE, read what the syllabus recommends as prior learning, then fill gaps with the foundation chapters: Algebra from scratch, Physics from zero, Chemistry from zero and Biology from zero. Phase 1: Fix your foundations gives a checklist.

Honest workload notes

No A Level is easy at A* standard, but subjects are hard in different ways.

  • Mathematics demands fluent algebra and a lot of practice. Answers are right or wrong, so it needs less extended writing, which helps if English is your second language.
  • Further Mathematics roughly doubles your maths load. Take it only if you are strong at Maths and enjoy it; it also makes ordinary Maths feel easier.
  • Physics needs confident Maths and clear explanations of ideas, not just formulas.
  • Chemistry combines a large amount of content with calculations, and later topics build directly on earlier ones, so falling behind early is costly.
  • Biology has a large amount of content and precise vocabulary, with many longer written answers.
  • Essay subjects (History, English Literature, Economics, Business) need wide reading and plenty of writing practice. If English is not your first language, start practising timed writing early; it is entirely possible to reach the top grades.
  • Private candidates should check that their centre can run every part of the course, such as a science laboratory exam or coursework, before choosing.

Common mistakes

Common mistakeChoosing for the wrong reasons
  • Picking a subject because your friends take it or because you like one teacher.
  • Dropping Mathematics without checking: it is required or preferred for engineering, computer science, physics, economics and more.
  • Assuming you need the A Level of the same name: law, economics, psychology, business and computer science degrees rarely require it.
  • Taking Further Maths when your Maths is not yet secure.
  • Taking four or five subjects “to impress” and getting lower grades in all of them.
  • Choosing two very similar subjects, such as Business and Economics, without checking: some selective universities prefer them not to be two of your three.
Exam techniqueGrades matter as much as subjects

A university looks at both what you studied and how well you did. A subject you enjoy and can score an A in is usually a better choice than a “prestigious” one in which you would get a C, provided the required subjects for your course are covered.

Quick check
Summary
  • Work backwards: list possible degrees, check their required subjects, then choose subjects that satisfy all of them.
  • Medicine, dentistry and veterinary science need Chemistry and usually Biology; engineering needs Maths and usually Physics, with Further Maths strongly recommended.
  • Computer science and economics usually need Maths but rarely the A Level of the same name; law usually needs no particular subject.
  • Three A Levels is standard; a fourth makes most sense as Further Mathematics.
  • Maths plus one or two sciences keeps the most options open.
  • Schools usually expect a 6 or 7 (B or A) at GCSE/IGCSE in a subject, and higher for Further Maths.
  • Requirements differ between universities and change over time: always check the course page for your entry year.

Start Here/Welcome

How to use this guide

Start hereStudy time15 minutes

How Zero to A* is organised, what each type of box means, how to search, track your progress and use the tools, and a simple learning loop that turns every chapter into exam marks.

Why this matters

A guide only helps if you use it actively. Reading a chapter once feels productive, but most of it is forgotten within days. Working through it in the right order, and coming back to it later, is what turns reading into marks.

How the guide is organised

Open the menu (the ☰ button on a phone, or the sidebar on a larger screen) to see every subject: the six main subjects (Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Engineering and Business), Economics and Accounting, short guides to other subjects, the preparation road, the toolbox and practice quizzes. Each subject is split into groups of chapters in a sensible order of study, usually starting with a course map.

The top of each chapter shows a level label, a short summary and, for subject chapters, the exams that test it and a realistic study time for a beginner. The level labels mean:

Label What it means
Foundations GCSE/IGCSE skills that A Level assumes. Start here if you are rusty.
AS Level First-year content.
A Level (A2) Second-year content, needed for the full A Level.
Guide, Reference, Summary Course maps, the preparation road, formula sheets and short subject summaries.
Interactive Tools such as the graph plotter and calculators.
Beyond A Level Extension material, such as the tour of Further Mathematics.

Most chapters begin with Before you start links to the chapters you need first, and end with a Next link. On a wide screen, the On this page panel lists the sections and gives an estimated reading time.

The boxes, and how to use them

Box What it holds How to use it
Key term An exact definition in examiner-quality wording Learn it word for word: definitions are easy marks
Worked example A full solution, with marks shown in exam-style ones Cover the solution and try it first
Common mistake An error examiners see every year Check your own work against it
Exam technique What a question wants and where the marks are Apply it when you practise past papers
Board differences Where Edexcel International, AQA or OCR differ from Cambridge Read the parts for your board
Tip, Think of it like this Shortcuts and everyday analogies Use them to understand, then learn the precise version
Key facts, Formula Facts and formulas to memorise Turn them into flashcards
Practical skills Methods, apparatus, safety and errors in experiments Essential for practical and planning papers
Try it yourself Practice questions, each with a hidden full answer Attempt first; only then press Show answer
Quick check Multiple-choice questions marked instantly Read the explanation every time, even when you are right
Summary The facts to remember from the chapter Test yourself on them a week later

Here is what three of them look like.

Mark scheme

The document examiners use to award marks. It lists the accepted answers and shows exactly where each mark is earned, including method (M), accuracy (A) and independent (B) marks in Mathematics.

Worked exampleA rectangle is (x+3) cm long and x cm wide. Its area is 40 cm2. Find x.

Form the equation: x(x+3)=40, so x2+3x−40=0. B1

Factorise: (x+8)(x−5)=0. M1

So x=5; reject x=−8, because a length cannot be negative. A1

Check: a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide has area 40 cm2.

The mark labels follow the system used in Cambridge and Edexcel mathematics mark schemes:

  • M (method): for a correct method applied to the problem, even if you then make a slip.
  • A (accuracy): for a correct answer or step. You can only earn it if you have earned the method mark it depends on.
  • B (independent): for a correct result or statement that does not depend on a method.

So a correct answer with no working may not earn full marks, while a wrong answer with a sound method can still earn some. You will meet problems like this one in Quadratics.

Common mistakeReading is not the same as doing

Following a worked solution feels easy because every step is already there. The real test is whether you can produce it yourself with the page covered. Always try first, then compare.

Track your progress

At the end of every chapter there is a Mark as learned button. Press it when you can do the practice questions without help. Learned chapters get a tick in the menu, the progress bar fills up, and the home page shows how many chapters you have learned in each subject, with a link to pick up where you left off.

Common mistakeProgress is saved in this browser only

Your ticks, theme and text size are stored on this device, in this browser. They do not move between your phone and your computer, and clearing your browsing data or using a private window removes them. Choose one main device for studying.

Search, glossary, tools and display

  • Search: press / from anywhere (or tap the search box) and type a topic, key term or formula name. Use the arrow keys and Enter to open a result, or Esc to close the list.
  • Glossary: every key-term card in the guide, in one alphabetical list that you can filter by subject: Glossary.
  • Tools: the graph plotter, the periodic table, calculators for UCAS points, formula masses, break-even and more, and formula sheets such as the maths formula sheet.
  • Practice: Practice quizzes mix questions from every chapter and tell you which chapters to revise.
  • Planning: Build your personal study plan turns your exam date into a weekly timetable.
  • Display: the buttons at the top right switch between light and dark mode and cycle the text size from normal to large to extra large.

The learning loop

Use the same six steps for every chapter.

  1. Read the chapter with pen and paper. Write each key term in your own words, then compare it with the card.
  2. Study the worked examples. Cover each solution, attempt it, then compare, noting where the marks are.
  3. Try it yourself with the chapter closed. Open Show answer only after a real attempt, and mark your work honestly.
  4. Take the quick check and read every explanation.
  5. Mark as learned only when you can do the practice questions without help.
  6. Revisit after a week. Redo a few questions and the quick check from memory. Each time you pull an idea back out of memory after a gap, you keep it for longer.
TipLittle and often

A main-subject chapter usually takes several sessions, as its study time shows. End each session by writing down three things you learned, and start the next one by recalling them without notes.

Use the guide with your syllabus, a textbook and past papers

Resource Use it for When
This guide Learning each topic from zero, worked examples, practice Throughout the course
Official syllabus The final word on what can be examined At the start, then as a checklist
A textbook written for your syllabus Extra explanations and more questions Alongside each chapter
Past papers, mark schemes, examiner reports Real exam questions and how they are marked Topic questions from the start; full timed papers in the final months

Download the syllabus for your board and exam year from the board’s website and tick off each learning outcome as you finish it. Facts in this guide were checked in October 2026, but if anything here disagrees with your official syllabus, the syllabus wins. For recommended books and websites, see The best resources by subject; for a past-paper method, see Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes.

Try it yourselfCheck you know your way around

  1. In a mark scheme, what is the difference between an M mark and an A mark?

    Show answer

    An M mark is for a correct method applied to the problem. An A mark is for an accurate answer or step, and it can only be awarded if the method mark it depends on has been earned.

  2. You have just read a chapter and its worked examples. What should you do next, and why?

    Show answer

    Try the practice questions with the chapter closed, and only then check the answers. Recognising a solution is much easier than producing one, and producing answers from memory is what builds lasting understanding.

Quick check
Summary
  • Each subject is split into chapters labelled Foundations, AS Level or A Level (A2), with the exams that test them and a realistic study time.
  • Key-term cards hold exact definitions; worked examples show marks: M for method, A for accuracy (dependent on M), B for independent results.
  • Common-mistake, exam-technique and board-difference boxes show where marks are lost and how the boards differ.
  • Try it yourself hides full answers; quick checks mark you instantly and explain why.
  • Press / to search. The glossary, tools, formula sheets, practice quizzes and study planner are in the menu.
  • Progress, theme and text size are saved in this browser only.
  • The learning loop: read, study the worked examples, try without looking, quick check, mark as learned, revisit after a week.
  • Use the guide alongside the official syllabus, a textbook and past papers.

Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

The preparation road at a glance

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy time20 minutes to read

Six phases take you from your first day of study to results day. This page shows what each phase is for, how long it takes on three different timelines, the milestones you must not miss, and how to know when you are ready to move on.

Why this matters

Two years, or even one, is a long time, and long projects fail in a predictable way: weeks drift past, the hard topics get pushed back, and past papers start far too late. A road with clear phases turns one big, frightening goal into small weekly jobs. It also tells you what to do next on any given day, which is half the battle when you study alone.

The six phases

Every successful exam preparation, whatever the subject or board, passes through the same six phases. They are not strict boxes. Learning and practice run side by side, and past-paper work starts before the last topic is finished. But the order matters: you cannot practise what you have not learned, and timed papers only help once you know most of the content.

Phase What you do Why it matters How long
1. Fix your foundations Check and repair the GCSE/IGCSE skills each subject assumes: algebra, units, graphs, essay writing Every A Level topic is built on them, and small gaps slow down everything later 2–6 weeks
2. Learn the content Work through the syllabus topic by topic: read actively, make notes, follow worked examples You cannot practise or revise what you never understood About half of your total time
3. Practise and test yourself Retrieval practice, spaced review, flashcards, topic questions, an error log Understanding fades within days unless you test it; testing makes it stick Alongside phase 2, then 3–6 weeks of its own
4. Past papers Real papers under timed conditions, marked honestly with the official mark scheme Teaches the exam’s style, its timing and the wording that earns marks 8–12 weeks
5. Final revision Condense notes, target weak topics, sit full mock exams Turns what you know into marks you can rely on under pressure The last 6–8 weeks
6. Exam day Prepare the logistics, manage your time in the paper, then deal with results, reviews and resits Avoids losing marks to nerves, admin or a missing plan B The exam series and results day

Three tracks: how long each phase takes

How long you spend in each phase depends on how much time you have. The three most common situations are below. Find yours, then use the study planner to turn it into dated weeks.

2-year school route 12-month intensive 5–6-month resit or crash plan
Who it suits Students in Years 12–13 at a school or college Private candidates studying full-time, often straight after IGCSE Students resitting, or who already know much of the content
Typical dates September of Year 12 → May/June of Year 13 June → June, or October → October/November of the next year June → October/November, or December → May/June
1. Foundations 3–4 weeks (the summer before, plus September) 3–4 weeks 1 week: a diagnostic test only
2. Learn September of Year 12 to about February of Year 13 26–30 weeks 4–8 weeks, weak topics only
3. Practise Every week, plus about 4 weeks of consolidation Every week, plus about 3 weeks Every week: the main activity
4. Past papers Topic questions from Year 12; full papers January–April of Year 13 8–10 weeks 8–10 weeks
5. Final revision 8 weeks (April–May of Year 13) 6–8 weeks 3–4 weeks
6. Exam day May/June; results in August Your chosen series Your chosen series
Study outside lessons 10–15 hours a week 30–36 hours a week 8–12 hours a week per subject
Board differencesStaged, linear and modular

Cambridge International lets you take the AS papers at the end of Year 12 and the rest of the A Level a year later (staged assessment). An AS result can be carried forward for up to 13 months. If your school works this way, you run phases 4–6 twice: a short version for AS in Year 12, then the full version in Year 13. AQA and OCR A Levels are linear: every paper is sat in May/June at the end of the course. Edexcel International A Levels (IAL) are modular, with exams in January, May/June and October, so you can sit some units early and spread the load.

Milestones you must not miss

When Milestone Details
Before you start Choose your subjects and board, and download the syllabus for your exam year Choosing your subjects, Exam boards
First month (private candidates) Find an exam centre; ask about entry deadlines, fees and practical papers In Turkey: the British Council (Istanbul, Ankara) and Pearson-approved schools. See Studying as a private candidate
Every 6–8 weeks A timed test on everything learned so far Record the score in your progress tracker
Autumn of your final year University applications UCAS deadlines for 2027 entry: 15 October 2026 (Oxford, Cambridge and most medicine, dentistry and veterinary courses), 13 January 2027 (most other courses). See University applications
Several months before the exams Exam entries close Schools enter you; private candidates enter through their centre. Late entries cost extra
2–4 months before the first paper Mock exams A full set of papers in exam conditions
Start of phase 5 Past-paper target At least 5 full papers per component done and marked; 8–12 by exam day
August (for June exams) Results day Cambridge results for the June 2026 series came out on 11 August 2026

How many hours a week?

Cambridge designs each A Level around 360 guided learning hours of teaching (about 180 for an AS Level). That is class time with a teacher; practice and revision come on top. As a rough guide:

  • At school: lessons plus 3–5 hours of your own study per subject per week, so 10–15 hours a week for three subjects. Raise this to 20 or more in the final 8 weeks.
  • Private candidate, full-time: 10–12 hours per subject per week, so 30–36 hours for three subjects. Treat it like a job: a fixed start time, fixed breaks, and one day a week off.
  • Resitting one or two subjects: 8–12 hours per subject per week.
TipHours are not the goal

Two hours of testing yourself beat five hours of rereading. Track your hours to make sure the time goes in, but judge your progress by your scores on questions you have not seen before.

Are you ready to move on?

Use these checks at the end of each phase. If you fail one, do not panic: spend another week or two on that phase, then check again.

Phase You are ready to move on when…
1. Foundations You score at least 8 out of 10 on each foundation self-check without looking anything up
2. Learn For every syllabus learning outcome, you can explain the idea aloud and answer a basic question without notes
3. Practise You score 70% or more on mixed topic questions a week after learning them, and the same mistakes have stopped appearing in your error log
4. Past papers Your last three full papers, timed and honestly marked, reach your target grade
5. Final revision Every topic in your tracker is green, and you can write out the key formulas and definitions from memory
Common mistakeThe commonest way to fall behind: living in phase 2

Many students spend months rereading notes and making them prettier, then reach the exam having answered almost no questions. Rereading feels productive because everything looks familiar, but recognising an idea is not the same as being able to use it. From the first week, end every study session with questions you answer without looking.

Exam techniqueStart from the syllabus, finish with the mark scheme

Two documents define what you need: the syllabus (what can be asked) and the mark schemes (what earns marks). Download the syllabus for your exam year before you study anything. Read your first mark scheme early, during phase 2, so you know what examiners look for from the start.

TipAlready part-way through?

You do not have to start at phase 1. If your exams are four months away, do one past paper per subject this week, mark it, and study the results. Then jump to the phase that fixes your biggest problem, and use the 5–6-month track for timing.

Where to go next

Start by building your personal study plan, then follow the phases in order, beginning with Phase 1: Fix your foundations. Along the way, read Study methods that actually work, Exam technique and Motivation, sleep and stress.

Summary
  • Six phases: fix foundations, learn, practise, past papers, final revision, exam day. They overlap, but the order matters.
  • Pick your track: the 2-year school route, the 12-month intensive, or the 5–6-month resit or crash plan.
  • Download the syllabus for your exam year first, and read a mark scheme early.
  • Private candidates: find an exam centre and check its entry deadlines in the first month.
  • Cambridge designs an A Level around 360 guided learning hours of teaching; your own practice comes on top.
  • Judge progress by scores on unseen questions, not by hours or pages of notes.
  • Move on from a phase only when you pass its “ready” check.

Next: Build your personal study plan.

PreviousHow to use this guideNextBuild your personal study plan
Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Build your personal study plan

InteractiveExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy time30 minutes

Turn the six phases into a dated, week-by-week plan for your own exam date and subjects. Then learn how to read the plan, adapt it when life gets in the way, and fill in a weekly timetable, with three complete example plans.

A good plan answers two questions: is my goal realistic? and what should I do this week? Enter your exam date and your subjects below. The planner counts the weeks you have and spreads them across the six phases, so you can see when each phase should start and finish.

TipWhich date should I enter?

Use the date of your first paper, not the last, because final revision has to be finished by then. If the timetable is not published yet, take the earliest date in your board’s window for that exam series. Planning for a week too early is harmless; planning for a week too late is not.

Build or check a plan by hand

The planner does the arithmetic, but you should understand it so that you can check the result, or redo it with a pen and a calendar.

  1. Count the whole weeks from next Monday to your first paper.
  2. Keep about one week in ten free as a buffer for illness, holidays and family events.
  3. Working back from the exam, mark the last 6–8 weeks as final revision (phase 5) and the 4–6 weeks before that as full past papers (phase 4).
  4. Mark the first 2–4 weeks as foundations (phase 1).
  5. The weeks left in the middle are for learning (phase 2), with practice (phase 3) built into every week. Share them between your subjects’ topics.
  6. Add the fixed dates: entry deadline, mocks, holidays and UCAS deadlines.

Then do a reality check. Each chapter of this guide shows a study time at the top (for example, 6–8 hours for Quadratics). Add about half as much again for practice, multiply by the number of topics, and compare the total with the hours your learning weeks give you. If it does not fit, you have three honest choices: study more hours a week, take fewer subjects in this series, or move to a later series. Never solve the problem by cutting phases 4 and 5, because that is where grades are made.

How to read your plan

  • Phase dates are targets, not walls. Phases overlap. Start past-paper questions on each topic as soon as you finish it, long before phase 4 officially begins.
  • The learning weeks are the tightest. If your plan gives you fewer than about 10 weeks per subject to learn the content, you are on an intensive track, and your weekly hours matter more than anything else.
  • Phase 5 has a minimum. Even a short plan needs at least 3–4 weeks of final revision.

Adapting the plan

Every plan goes wrong at some point. What matters is how you respond.

Situation What to do
1–2 weeks behind Use a buffer week, or add 3–5 hours a week for a month. Do not push every later phase back
3 or more weeks behind Decide now: more hours, one subject moved to the next series, or an AS Level only this time (a Cambridge AS Level is a qualification in its own right)
Ahead of schedule Do more mixed practice and past-paper questions; do not race ahead to new content
A topic takes twice as long as planned Normal for hard topics. Borrow time from a buffer week, never from practice
Ill or away for a week Restart with a weekly review; do not try to “catch up” by working through the night

Run the planner again once a month: it shows whether you are on track while there is still time to act.

Common mistakeA plan with no spare time breaks in week three

If every hour of every week is filled, the first cold or family wedding pushes everything back, and the plan starts to feel like a list of failures. Leave buffer weeks, keep one day a week free, and plan only the next week in detail.

Three example plans

A. School student: Year 12 from September 2026, exams in June 2028

Term Main phases Targets and milestones
Autumn 2026 (Year 12) 1 in September, then 2 and 3 Foundation self-checks in the first 3 weeks; weekly reviews from October; first unit tests in November
Spring 2027 2 and 3, plus past-paper questions by topic Most AS content finished by Easter
Summer 2027 AS exams in May/June if your school uses staged assessment; otherwise school exams Start the A Level content in June; in the holidays, research universities and draft your personal statement
Autumn 2027 (Year 13) 2 and 3 for the A Level content UCAS: mid-October deadline for Oxford, Cambridge and medicine, January for most courses; admissions tests
Spring 2028 Content finished by February; mocks; then 4 From February, 1–2 timed papers per subject per week; at least 5 per component by Easter
Summer 2028 5 (the 8 weeks before your first paper), then 6 Exams in May/June; results in August 2028

B. Private candidate: October 2026 to June 2027, Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry

A full-time candidate studying about 36 hours a week for Cambridge 9709, 9702 and 9701 in the May/June 2027 series. Week 1 starts on Monday 5 October 2026, and the plan assumes a first paper in early May.

Weeks Dates Phase Mathematics 9709 Physics 9702 Chemistry 9701
1–2 5–18 Oct 1 Algebra, powers, graphs Units, standard form, rearranging Formulas, equations, basic moles
3–8 19 Oct – 29 Nov 2 + 3 Pure 1 AS topics 1–6 AS topics 1–8
9–12 30 Nov – 27 Dec 2 + 3 Pure 3, first half AS topics 7–11 AS topics 9–16
13 28 Dec – 3 Jan Buffer Rest and catch up Rest and catch up Rest and catch up
14–17 4–31 Jan 2027 2 + 3 Pure 3, second half A Level topics 12–18 AS 17–22, A Level 23–26
18–21 1–28 Feb 2 + 3 Probability & Statistics 1, Mechanics A Level topics 19–25 A Level topics 27–37
22–25 1–28 Mar 4 Two timed papers a week Timed papers; Paper 5 planning practice Timed papers; Paper 5 planning practice
26–30 29 Mar – 2 May 5 Final revision; full mocks in weeks 26 and 29 As Maths As Maths
31 on From 3 May 6 Exams Exams Exams
Common mistakeThis plan is intensive

Thirty weeks of 36 hours gives about 360 hours per subject: the same as Cambridge’s guided learning hours, but without a teacher. It suits students with strong IGCSE grades in all three subjects who can study full-time. If you are more than two weeks behind in week 8, move your weakest subject to the October/November 2027 series. Cambridge science candidates also sit a practical exam (Paper 3), so check early that your centre can run it, and book some laboratory practice before March.

C. Resit student: sitting again in November

Emre sat A Level Chemistry in June 2027 and knows that Paper 4 went badly. He needs an A for a university application next year, so he starts preparing for the October/November 2027 series the week after his last June paper. Waiting for results day in August would cost him eight weeks. He plans 10–12 hours a week.

Weeks When Phase Focus
1 Late June 1: diagnosis One paper of each component done cold and marked; every topic sorted into red, amber or green; ask the centre for the November entry deadline
2–7 July to mid-August 2 + 3 Relearn two red topics a week; daily flashcards; topic questions after each one
Results day August – Confirm the grade; ask the centre about a copy of the marked script; make sure the November entry is in
8–13 Mid-August to late September 4 One or two timed papers a week, marked the same day; every lost mark redone a week later
14–17 October 5 Amber topics, condensed notes, two full mocks
18 on October/November 6 The exams; results in January

A weekly timetable template

Copy this pattern into a notebook or calendar and adapt it to your subjects. Each day mixes new learning with practice on earlier topics, and every week ends with a review.

Day Private candidate, full-time (about 36 hours) School student (about 9 hours, plus homework)
Monday 09:00–12:00 Maths, new topic · 13:30–16:30 Physics, new topic · 20 min flashcards 1 hour: redo today’s lesson examples without looking · 20 min flashcards
Tuesday Chemistry, new topic · Maths, questions on Monday’s topic · flashcards 1 hour Chemistry questions · 20 min flashcards
Wednesday Physics, questions · Chemistry, questions · flashcards 1 hour Physics questions · 20 min flashcards
Thursday Maths, new topic · Physics, new topic · flashcards 1 hour Maths questions · 20 min error log
Friday Chemistry, new topic · mixed questions from all three · flashcards Free evening
Saturday 09:00–12:00 one timed test or past-paper section · 30 min marking it and updating the error log 2–3 hours: one timed section, marked; catch up
Sunday 45 min weekly review and plan; the rest of the day free 45 min weekly review and plan; homework
Exam techniquePlan around the exam timetable

When the timetable is published, mark every paper on your plan. Note which paper comes first in each subject and any days with two papers. Then arrange your last two weeks in the same order, so the paper you sit first gets the first final mock.

Summary
  • Enter the date of your first paper; if the timetable is not out yet, use the earliest date of the exam series window.
  • Work back from the exam: final revision, then past papers, then learning. Keep about one week in ten as a buffer.
  • Reality-check the learning weeks: each chapter’s study time plus half again for practice, times the number of topics.
  • If you fall 3 or more weeks behind, decide early: more hours, a later series for one subject, or AS only.
  • Never shorten phases 4 and 5 to rescue phase 2.
  • Review every Sunday and re-run the planner once a month.
