Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 1: Fix your foundations

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy time2–6 weeks (this phase)

Every A Level assumes skills from GCSE or IGCSE. This phase checks those skills with a short self-test and repairs the gaps before they slow you down. It also covers the academic English that second-language learners need.

Why this matters

Most students who struggle at A Level do not struggle with the new ideas. They struggle because an old skill is shaky: rearranging a formula, handling a negative number, writing a clear paragraph. Every new topic then takes twice as long, and the student concludes “I’m not good at this subject” when the real problem is a two-hour gap from three years ago. A few weeks spent on foundations now saves months later.

What each A Level assumes

Cambridge writes its AS and A Level syllabuses for students who have studied the subject at IGCSE or GCSE (or an equivalent course). You do not need a top grade, but the core skills must be quick and reliable, because at A Level they are tools inside bigger problems, not the problem itself.

Mathematics, and the maths inside the sciences

Skill You should be able to… Repair it here
Number Work with fractions, negative numbers, percentages and ratios without a calculator Numbers, fractions and percentages
Algebra Expand and factorise; solve linear and simultaneous equations; rearrange formulas Algebra from scratch
Powers Use the laws of indices, simplify surds, work in standard form Powers, roots, surds and standard form
Graphs Find a gradient, use y=mx+c, plot points and read values from a graph Coordinates and straight lines
Geometry Use Pythagoras’ theorem, sine, cosine and tangent, angle facts, areas and volumes Geometry and basic trigonometry

Physics, Chemistry and Biology

The sciences use five maths skills constantly, so check these even if Mathematics is not one of your subjects.

  • Units and prefixes: converting mm to m, kJ to J, cm3 to dm3, and knowing that 1 dm3=1000 cm3.
  • Rearranging: making any letter the subject of a formula such as pV=nRT or v2=u2+2as.
  • Standard form: writing 0.000 045 6 as 4.56×10−5 and entering it correctly on a calculator.
  • Significant figures: giving an answer to the same number of significant figures as the data, usually 2 or 3.
  • Graphs: choosing scales, drawing a line of best fit, and finding a gradient from a large triangle.

Each science also has its own starting knowledge: atoms, ions and equations in Chemistry; forces, energy and circuits in Physics; cells, organs and basic genetics in Biology. Check and repair these with Physics from zero, Chemistry from zero and Biology from zero.

Business, Economics and other essay subjects

Essay subjects assume you can read a long case study quickly, pick out the useful facts and numbers, calculate a percentage change, and write a clear paragraph that makes one point and explains it. No prior Business or Economics course is needed, but if these skills feel slow, start with Business from zero and Writing top-band business answers.

The ten-minute self-check

Do these without a calculator or notes. Give yourself one mark for each fully correct answer. Score 8 or more and you can start phase 2; otherwise, repair the skills you missed first, using the links above.

Try it yourselfFoundation self-check (Mathematics and sciences)

  1. Work out 23+34.

    Show answer

    Use a common denominator of 12: 812+912=1712, which is 1512.

  2. Expand and simplify (2x−3)(x+4).

    Show answer

    2x2+8x−3x−12=2x2+5x−12.

  3. Factorise x2−7x+12.

    Show answer

    Two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to −7 are −3 and −4, so (x−3)(x−4).

  4. Make u the subject of v2=u2+2as.

    Show answer

    u2=v2−2as, so u=±v2−2as.

  5. Solve the simultaneous equations 2x+y=7 and x−y=2.

    Show answer

    Adding them gives 3x=9, so x=3. Then y=7−2(3)=1.

  6. Simplify x5×x−2x2.

    Show answer

    Add the powers when multiplying and subtract when dividing: x5−2−2=x1=x.

  7. Write 0.000 045 6 in standard form, and give 0.004 562 to 2 significant figures.

    Show answer

    4.56×10−5 and 0.0046.

  8. Convert 250 mm to metres, 3.5 kW to watts, and 250 cm3 to dm3.

    Show answer

    0.25 m, 3500 W and 0.25 dm3 (because 1 dm3=1000 cm3).

  9. Find the gradient and the y-intercept of the line 2y−6x=8.

    Show answer

    Rearrange to y=3x+4: the gradient is 3 and the line crosses the y-axis at (0,4).

  10. A price rises from $40 to $46. Find the percentage increase.

    Show answer

    The increase is $6, and 640×100=15%.

For essay subjects, the check is a list of “I can” statements. Be honest: tick one only if you could do it today, under time pressure.

  • I can read a one-page article in English in under five minutes and summarise it in three sentences.
  • I can write a paragraph that makes one point, explains why, and gives an example.
  • I can calculate a percentage change and say what it means in words.
  • I can read a simple table or chart and describe the trend with numbers.
  • I can define ten basic terms in my subject (for Business: profit, revenue, costs, market, stakeholder and so on) in one sentence each.

Academic English for second-language learners

Every paper is set and marked in English, and many students who know the science well lose marks to language. The good news: exam English is a small, learnable language of its own.

  • Learn the command words. “Describe” (say what happens) and “explain” (say why it happens) earn different marks. See Command words decoded.
  • Keep a vocabulary notebook. Four columns: the English term, the word in your own language, the definition in English, and an example sentence. Learn definitions as fixed phrases, exactly as the syllabus words them.
  • Write short, complete sentences. Examiners reward correct science and clear reasoning, not elegant style. One idea per sentence is safer than one long sentence with three ideas.
  • Read in English every day. Fifteen minutes of your textbook or a good subject website builds reading speed, which matters in long case-study and data questions.
  • Use the glossary in this guide: every key term from every chapter is collected there.
English term Turkish Definition in English
gradient eğim the change in y divided by the change in x
dynamic equilibrium dinamik denge forward and reverse reactions happen at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant
demand talep the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price
evaluate değerlendirmek judge the strengths and weaknesses, then reach a conclusion
Common mistake“I got an A at IGCSE, so I can skip this”

Skills fade, especially over a long summer, and A Level needs them to be fast as well as correct. Do the self-check anyway: it takes ten minutes, and it either confirms you are ready or finds a gap while it is still cheap to fix.

Exam techniqueFoundation skills carry marks in every paper

A correct method with a slip in rearranging, a wrong power of ten or a missing unit can still lose the final accuracy mark. In Cambridge Mathematics, a non-exact answer not given to 3 significant figures (unless the question asks otherwise) can also cost marks. Examiners usually accept small spelling mistakes, but not when the misspelt word could be another technical term, such as ethane and ethene, or mitosis and meiosis.

How long should phase 1 take?

Your self-check result Plan
8–10, and quick About 2 weeks: repair anything you missed and read the “from zero” chapter for each science, then start phase 2
6–7 3–4 weeks: work through the foundation chapters for every skill you missed, then redo the self-check
5 or fewer, or no IGCSE in the subject 5–6 weeks: work through all the foundation chapters for that subject in order
Any score, if English is your second language Add 15 minutes of subject reading in English every day, all the way to the exam
TipFix the core now, the rest just in time

You do not need to repair everything before you start learning. Fix the core skills now (algebra, rearranging, units, paragraph writing), then repair smaller gaps as topics need them. Every chapter in this guide begins with a “Before you start” line that links to exactly what it assumes.

Summary
  • Most A Level difficulty comes from shaky GCSE/IGCSE skills, not from the new ideas.
  • Maths skills to check: number, algebra, powers and standard form, graphs, geometry and trigonometry.
  • Science skills to check: units and prefixes, rearranging, standard form, significant figures, graphs.
  • Essay subjects need fast reading, clear paragraphs and confident use of data.
  • Score 8 out of 10 on the self-check before moving on; repair what you missed with the foundation chapters.
  • Second-language learners: learn the command words, keep a four-column vocabulary notebook and read in English daily.
  • Phase 1 takes 2–6 weeks, depending on your score.

Next: Phase 2: Learn the content.

PreviousBuild your personal study planNextPhase 2: Learn the content
Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 2: Learn the content

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy timeAbout half of your preparation time

How to work through the syllabus so that the ideas stay: studying each chapter actively, turning the syllabus into a checklist, making notes that help, choosing a textbook, keeping a steady pace, and getting unstuck.

Why this matters

Phase 2 is the longest part of the road, and the easiest to get wrong. Reading a chapter is not the same as learning it. You have learned a topic when you can explain it and use it without looking, a week later. Everything in this phase is designed to get you to that point with as little wasted time as possible.

How to study one chapter actively

Passive study (reading, highlighting, copying) feels comfortable because the material looks familiar while it is in front of you. Active study makes your brain produce the ideas itself, which is harder in the moment and far more effective. Use this routine for every chapter in this guide or your textbook.

  1. Preview (5 minutes). Read the summary, the headings and the key-term cards. Ask yourself what the topic is for.
  2. Study one section at a time. At the end of each section, look away and explain it aloud or on paper in your own words.
  3. Work through each worked example with the solution covered. Attempt each step before you reveal it.
  4. Answer the practice questions without notes, then check them against the full answers and mark honestly.
  5. Write your notes from memory, then compare them with the chapter and fill the gaps in a different colour.
  6. Finish with the quick check, and make flashcards from the key terms and formulas.

Work in focused blocks of 25–50 minutes with a short break between them, and keep your phone in another room. The timer below helps.

Turn the syllabus into a checklist

The syllabus for your exam year is the official list of everything that can be examined. Download it free from your board’s website. In the subject content section, each topic is broken into numbered learning outcomes, short statements of what you must be able to do. Copy them into a tracker, in a notebook or a spreadsheet, and colour each one as you go.

Learning outcome (Quadratics, Cambridge Paper 1, in our words) Learned Practised Exam-ready
Complete the square and use it to find the vertex Yes Yes Green
Use the discriminant to decide how many real roots there are Yes Yes Amber
Solve quadratic inequalities Yes No Red
Solve one linear and one quadratic equation simultaneously No No Red
  • Red: not learned yet, or you cannot do it even with notes.
  • Amber: you can do it with notes, or slowly.
  • Green: you can do it without notes, under time pressure, at least a week after learning it.

The tracker becomes the backbone of your whole preparation. In phase 5 it tells you exactly which topics need work.

Making notes that help

Good notes are short, written partly from memory, and built for testing yourself later. Three formats work well. Use whichever suits the topic.

Method How it works Best for
Cornell notes A page split into a cue column, a notes column and a summary strip First notes on a topic: definitions, explanations, methods
Concept map The main idea in the centre, with branches and labelled links Connections: organic reactions, the cardiovascular system, macroeconomic policy
One-page summary One sheet per topic: key terms, formulas, one diagram, one worked example, common mistakes The end of a topic, and final revision
Common mistakeNotes are not the goal

Beautiful notes with colours and perfect handwriting take hours and teach little. If you are copying sentences from the textbook, stop. Close the book, write what you remember, then check. Notes are a tool for testing yourself, not a product.

Choosing a textbook

One good textbook per subject, this guide and the past papers are enough. Collecting more resources feels productive, but it is usually a way of avoiding practice.

  • Cambridge: look for books that carry Cambridge’s endorsement mark on the cover. Cambridge lists endorsed resources on its website, from publishers such as Cambridge University Press and Hodder Education.
  • Edexcel IAL: Pearson publishes its own student books for the IAL specifications.
  • AQA and OCR: each board approves or endorses textbooks from several publishers for its own specifications.
  • Check the syllabus years. A book written for an older syllabus can miss new topics or include ones that were removed. Compare its contents with the current syllabus before you buy, especially second-hand.

Pacing: how fast should you go?

Your plan from the study planner gives you a number of learning weeks. Divide the topics by the weeks to get your weekly target. For Cambridge, the number of topics in the syllabus is:

Subject (Cambridge) Topics or sections Topics per week with 20 learning weeks
Mathematics 9709 (Pure 1, Pure 3, Mechanics, Probability & Statistics 1) 8 + 9 + 5 + 5 = 27 about 1.4
Physics 9702 25 (1–11 AS, 12–25 A Level) about 1.3
Chemistry 9701 37 (1–22 AS, 23–37 A Level) about 1.9
Biology 9700 19 (1–11 AS, 12–19 A Level) about 1

Topics differ in size, so treat these as averages. Study all your subjects every week rather than one subject per month: switching between subjects is tiring at first, but it gives each topic time to settle and keeps every subject fresh. If a topic takes more than one and a half times its budget, mark it amber, move on, and come back to it in your buffer week.

Flashcards as you go

Make flashcards on the day you finish each chapter, while you still know what matters. Aim for 5–15 cards per chapter:

  • one fact per card, written as a question: “What is the discriminant of ax2+bx+c?”
  • definitions word for word on the back, exactly as the syllabus uses them;
  • “why” questions as well as “what” questions: “Why does the rate of reaction increase with temperature?”

Paper cards in a box or a free flashcard app both work. How and when to review them is in Phase 3.

The weekly review

Once a week, for 30–45 minutes, step back from new content.

  1. Test yourself for 15 minutes, without notes, on this week’s topics and one older topic.
  2. Update the colours in your tracker.
  3. Read your error log: is any mistake appearing again and again?
  4. Compare where you are with your plan, and write next week’s topics into your timetable.

When you are stuck

Being stuck is a normal part of learning, not a sign that you cannot do the subject. Work down this list.

  1. Slow down. Reread the section, then copy out the worked example line by line, asking why each step follows from the one before.
  2. Go back one step. Most stuck points are really an earlier gap. Follow the “Before you start” link at the top of the chapter.
  3. Find a different explanation: your textbook, a video, or a friend who explains it in other words.
  4. Ask a precise question. “I don’t understand moles” is hard to answer; “I don’t see why we divide by 2 in line 3” is easy. Teachers, study groups and online forums all respond better to precise questions.
  5. Set a time limit. After 30 minutes stuck, mark the topic red, move on, and return in two days. Sleep often does the work for you.
TipExplain it to a younger student

If you can explain a topic simply to someone two years younger, without notes, you understand it. If you get stuck halfway, you have found exactly the part to study again.

Exam techniqueLearn definitions word for word

Definitions are quick marks, and mark schemes look for precise key words. “Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity” scores; “acceleration is how fast something speeds up” does not. Put every definition from the syllabus and from this guide’s key-term cards onto flashcards, and practise writing them out exactly.

Summary
  • Learning means being able to explain and use an idea without looking, a week later.
  • Study each chapter actively: preview, explain each section, attempt worked examples before reading them, answer questions without notes.
  • Turn the syllabus learning outcomes into a red/amber/green tracker.
  • Use Cornell notes, concept maps or one-page summaries; write notes from memory.
  • Use one endorsed textbook per subject that matches your syllabus years.
  • Pace yourself: divide topics by learning weeks, and study every subject every week.
  • Make flashcards on the day you finish a chapter, and review your week every weekend.

Next: Phase 3: Practise and test yourself.

PreviousPhase 1: Fix your foundationsNextPhase 3: Practise and test yourself
Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 3: Practise and test yourself

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy timeAlongside phase 2, then 3–6 weeks

Practice turns understanding into marks. This phase uses retrieval practice, spaced repetition, flashcards and mixed questions, with an error log that makes sure each mistake happens only once.

Why this matters

You can understand a topic perfectly on Monday and be unable to answer a question on it by Friday. Forgetting is normal, and it happens to everyone. The cure is not more reading: it is testing yourself, spread out over time. This phase runs alongside phase 2 from the first week, and becomes your main activity once all the content is learned.

Retrieval practice: test, don’t reread

Retrieval practice

Learning by recalling information from memory, for example by answering questions or writing down everything you remember, instead of reading the material again.

Every time you pull an idea out of memory, the memory becomes stronger and easier to find next time. Rereading does not do this, because the answer is already in front of you. A large 2013 review of ten common study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as the two most useful, and rereading and highlighting among the least useful.

Ways to practise retrieval:

  • Blank page: write everything you remember about a topic on a blank sheet, then check it against your notes and add what you missed in a different colour.
  • Flashcards, answered aloud or on paper before you turn the card over.
  • Quizzes: the quick check at the end of each chapter, and the mixed practice quizzes.
  • Exam-style questions, from your textbook, this guide and past papers.

Spaced repetition: when to review

Spaced repetition

Reviewing material at increasing intervals (for example after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days), so that each review happens just as the memory starts to fade.

Review a topic about 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days after you first learn it, then once a month until the exam. For example, for a topic learned on Monday 12 October 2026:

Review Day Date What to do (5–15 minutes)
1st 1 Tuesday 13 October Blank page, then check
2nd 3 Thursday 15 October Flashcards for the topic
3rd 7 Monday 19 October 3–4 exam-style questions
4th 14 Monday 26 October Quiz or mixed questions
5th 30 Wednesday 11 November A past-paper question, timed

Every review is a test, never a reread. If a review goes badly, restart the cycle for that topic from day 1. Write the review dates in your diary on the day you learn the topic, so you never have to remember them.

Flashcards that work

The Leitner system organises paper flashcards in five boxes. Box 1 is reviewed every day, box 2 every 3 days, box 3 every week, box 4 every 2 weeks and box 5 every month. A card you answer correctly moves up one box; a card you get wrong goes back to box 1. Flashcard apps such as Anki do the same scheduling automatically.

  • Answer before you flip. Say or write the full answer first. A vague “I knew that” counts as wrong.
  • Be strict. Half right is wrong for a definition, because the mark scheme wants the key words.
  • Mix card types: definitions, formulas, “why” questions, and blank diagrams to label.

Interleaving: mix your topics

Interleaving

Practising a mixture of different topics or question types in one session, so that you must decide which method each question needs, instead of practising one method many times in a row.

Blocked practice Interleaved practice
What it looks like 20 questions on completing the square 12 questions mixing quadratics, functions, series and trigonometry
How it feels Smooth and fast Slower and harder
What it trains Repeating a method you already know is needed Choosing the right method, which is what the exam demands
When to use it The first practice on a new topic Everything after that

Exam questions never tell you which chapter they come from. Once you have learned three or four topics, make most of your practice interleaved.

Topic questions

After each topic, climb this ladder: textbook exercises, then the practice questions in this guide, then past-paper questions on that topic. Collections of Cambridge questions sorted by topic (“topical past papers”) are widely available, and they let you practise a topic in exam style long before you sit full papers. Aim for at least 10–15 exam-style questions on each topic, more for big topics, before you call it green.

The error log

The error log is the most valuable document you will make. Every mark you lose goes into it, with the reason and a rule to stop it happening again.

Date Question Topic Marks lost What went wrong Type Rule for next time Redo on
12 Oct Maths practice Q4 Quadratics 2 Used −b=−4 when b=−4 Careless slip Write a, b, c with their signs before substituting 19 Oct
14 Oct Physics topic test Q2 Kinematics 2 Did not convert km h−1 to m s−1 Method Convert every quantity to SI units first 21 Oct
15 Oct Chemistry worksheet Q5 Moles 3 Ignored the 1 : 2 ratio in the equation Knowledge Always use the mole ratio from the balanced equation 22 Oct
20 Oct Business 12-mark question Motivation 4 No judgement at the end Exam technique End with a justified conclusion that answers the question 27 Oct

Use five types: knowledge (you did not know it), method (you knew the topic but chose or applied the wrong method), reading (you misread the question), careless slip, and exam technique (timing, missing working, no evaluation). Once a week, read the whole log and count the types. If most are knowledge errors, go back to phase 2 for those topics. If most are careless slips, slow down and check every answer. Then redo each logged question on its redo date, without looking at your old answer.

Calculation subjects and essay subjects

Calculations (Maths, Physics, Chemistry)
  • Do many questions: volume matters.
  • Write full working, as in the exam: method marks need visible steps.
  • Check units and significant figures at the end of every answer.
  • Redo wrong questions from a blank page, not by reading the solution.
  • Time yourself from early on: about 1.5 minutes per mark in Cambridge Maths.
Essays (Business, Economics, long-answer Biology)
  • Plan every answer for 3–5 minutes before writing.
  • Build each paragraph: knowledge, application, analysis, evaluation.
  • Write timed answers, then mark them against the mark scheme’s levels.
  • Collect strong chains of reasoning (“this leads to… which means…”).
  • See Writing top-band business answers.

Measuring readiness

Test each topic with mixed questions a week or more after learning it, and record your score.

Score Meaning What to do
80% or more Exam-ready Mark it green; review it once a month
60–79% Nearly there Mark it amber; work through its error-log entries and do more topic questions
Below 60% Not secure yet Mark it red; go back to the chapter (phase 2)

You are ready to give past papers most of your time when your average across mixed sets is 70% or more, no topic is red, and the same mistakes have stopped appearing in your error log.

TipStart every session with retrieval

Spend the first 10 minutes of each study session on questions or flashcards from older topics, before any new work. It warms you up, and it builds your spaced reviews into every day without extra planning.

Common mistakeLooking at the answer too soon

When a question gets hard, it is tempting to look at the solution after a minute. Struggle for at least 5–10 minutes first: the effort of trying is what makes the method stick. If you do look, close the solution and redo the whole question from a blank page.

Exam techniquePractise in exam format from the start

Write practice answers exactly as you would in the exam: full working, units, sentences rather than notes, and diagrams labelled. Habits formed in practice are the ones you will use under pressure, so make them exam habits from the first week.

Summary
  • Retrieval practice (testing yourself) beats rereading; use blank pages, flashcards, quizzes and exam-style questions.
  • Review each topic about 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days after learning it, then monthly; every review is a test.
  • Use a Leitner box or a flashcard app, and be strict with yourself.
  • Interleave: once you know a few topics, mix them in every practice set.
  • Keep an error log with a type and a rule for every lost mark, and redo each question a week later.
  • Green at 80% or more on mixed questions a week after learning; move on to past papers at a 70% average with no red topics.

Next: Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes.

PreviousPhase 2: Learn the contentNextPhase 4: Past papers and mark schemes
Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy time8–12 weeks

Where to find official past papers, mark schemes, examiner reports and grade thresholds; how many papers to do and in what order; how to sit them under timed conditions and mark them honestly; and the redo cycle that turns each lost mark into a gained one.

Why this matters

Past papers are the closest thing to the real exam that exists. They show you the style of the questions, how long you really need, and the exact ideas that earn marks. Students who do many past papers, mark them honestly and learn from every mistake usually outscore students who simply know more content.

Where to find them

Use the official sources first. Each board publishes four kinds of document for each exam series: question papers, mark schemes, examiner reports (what candidates did well and badly) and grade thresholds or grade boundaries (the raw marks needed for each grade).

Board Where to look Notes
Cambridge International The syllabus page on cambridgeinternational.org Cambridge publishes some past papers on its website. The full archive is on the School Support Hub, which registered schools use; private candidates can ask their exam centre
Pearson Edexcel (IAL) Your subject’s page on qualifications.pearson.com Papers, mark schemes and examiner reports under the exam materials; grade boundaries on their own page
AQA aqa.org.uk Past papers and mark schemes for each specification
OCR ocr.org.uk Past papers in the assessment section of each qualification

With every board, the newest series is sometimes available only to teachers for a while. Many other websites copy the official files. If you use one, make sure each paper comes with its matching mark scheme.

Reading Cambridge file names

Cambridge files have names like 9709_s25_qp_12. Once you can read them, finding the right paper takes seconds.

Part Meaning
9709 The syllabus code (Mathematics)
s25 The series and year: s = May/June, w = October/November, m = February/March; 25 = 2025
qp, ms, er, gt Question paper, mark scheme, examiner report, grade thresholds
12 Paper 1, variant 2

Cambridge sets several versions (variants) of most papers in each series for different time zones. That is why there are so many papers to practise with: a few recent years give you 20 or more versions of some components.

How many, and in what order?

Aim for 8–12 full papers per component by exam day, plus topic questions, and more for components you find hard. Use them in this order:

  1. Older papers (about 6–10 years old): cut into topic questions during phase 3.
  2. Middle years: full timed papers in phase 4.
  3. The two or three most recent series: saved for full mocks in phase 5.

Before you start, read the “changes to the syllabus” page at the front of your syllabus. Papers written before a syllabus change can include topics that are no longer examined, and miss new ones. Skip those questions, or replace them with questions from this guide.

Sitting a paper under timed conditions

  1. Choose the same time of day as the real exam, a quiet desk, and only the permitted equipment: pens, pencil, ruler, an allowed calculator, and the formula list or data booklet your board provides (for Cambridge Mathematics, the list called MF19).
  2. Put your phone in another room and set a timer for the real length of the paper.
  3. Read the front cover as if it were the real exam.
  4. Work to time. Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 has 75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes, so allow about 1.5 minutes per mark.
  5. When time runs out, draw a line. You may finish in a different colour to see what more time would give, but count only the marks above the line.

Marking honestly

Mark the paper the same day, or the next, with the official mark scheme. Be strict: if your answer does not clearly contain the point the mark scheme describes, do not give yourself the mark. Generous self-marking only hides the problems you need to fix.

Mathematics mark schemes use a short code. Learn it, because it tells you exactly how marks are earned:

Code Meaning
M1 A method mark, for a correct method applied to the problem
A1 An accuracy mark: only possible if the related M mark is earned
B1 An independent mark for a correct answer or statement
FT Follow through: credit for correct work that uses your own earlier wrong answer
CAO Correct answer only
OE Or equivalent: another correct form of the answer is accepted
AWRT Answer which rounds to the value given
AG Answer given in the question: every step must be shown

Science mark schemes list the acceptable answers for each mark point, and essay mark schemes describe levels: what an answer must show to reach each band of marks. Then turn your raw mark into a grade with the grade thresholds for that series and variant. Thresholds change from series to series because some papers are harder than others, so always use the matching one. Aim to be comfortably above your target grade, not just on it.

Exam techniqueWhy the method mark matters

An A mark depends on its M mark. A correct final answer from a wrong or invisible method can score nothing, while a wrong final answer from a correct method can still score most of the marks. In “show that” questions, the answer is printed (the mark scheme labels it AG), so all the marks are for the steps. Always write your working where the examiner can follow it.

Read the examiner report

For every paper you sit, read the examiner report’s comments on it. Examiners describe the common errors, the misunderstandings they saw most often, and what the best answers did. Ten minutes with the report often explains a lost mark better than the mark scheme does. Copy anything that applies to you into your error log.

Topic by topic, or full papers?

Topic-by-topic questions Full papers
When Phase 3 and the start of phase 4 Most of phase 4, and all of phase 5
What it trains Depth in one topic; finding gaps quickly Timing, stamina, switching between topics, choosing methods
The risk The topic heading tells you which method to use One paper cannot cover every topic

Use both. Start phase 4 with one full paper per component per week, plus topic sets for your weakest areas. Build up to two or three full papers a week in the last month of the phase.

The redo cycle

  1. Sit the paper, timed.
  2. Mark it honestly, the same day.
  3. Log every lost mark in your error log, with its type and a rule for next time.
  4. Relearn: for a knowledge gap, go back to the chapter; for a method gap, do three to five similar questions.
  5. Redo every question that lost marks, from a blank page, a week later.
  6. Track your scores for each component, with the grade thresholds next to them, so you can see the trend.
Common mistakeDo not memorise mark-scheme wording without understanding it

Mark schemes are written for examiners, not as model answers. Phrases learned by heart without understanding end up in the wrong context, where they earn nothing. Questions are reworded every year, and the mark is for the idea used correctly. Learn why each point earns its mark, then practise explaining it in your own words while keeping the key technical terms.

TipKeep the newest papers for later

Do not use the two or three most recent series before phase 5. They are the best guide to your own exam, so save them for full mocks under real conditions.

Summary
  • Use official sources: Cambridge (public website and the School Support Hub through your centre), Pearson, AQA and OCR, with mark schemes, examiner reports and grade thresholds.
  • Read Cambridge file names: syllabus, series and year, document type, paper and variant (9709_s25_qp_12).
  • Aim for 8–12 full papers per component: old papers as topic questions, middle years timed, newest saved for mocks.
  • Sit papers in real conditions and to time: about 1.5 minutes per mark in Cambridge Maths Paper 1.
  • Mark strictly; learn M, A, B, FT and AG; compare your mark with the thresholds for that exact paper.
  • Read the examiner report for every paper, and follow the redo cycle: sit, mark, log, relearn, redo, track.
  • Understand mark-scheme points; never memorise their wording blindly.

Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 5: Final revision

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy timeThe last 6–8 weeks

A week-by-week plan for the last eight weeks before your first paper, with daily timetables, how to run your own mocks, how to condense your notes, formula practice, sleep, and the habits to avoid.

Why this matters

The last eight weeks decide more grades than any other part of the course. By now you know most of the content; this phase makes it reliable under pressure. Done well, it is calm and organised: you know exactly what to do each day, and each week you can see the gaps closing.

The last eight weeks, week by week

Count the weeks back from your first paper. If you have only six weeks, combine weeks 8 and 7, and weeks 6 and 5.

Weeks to go Main focus Full papers per subject Also this week
8 Audit: update your tracker, list every red and amber topic, plan the eight weeks 1, as a baseline Get the final exam timetable and mark every paper on your plan
7 Red topics, first half: relearn, then practise 1 Condensed notes for each red topic
6 Red topics, second half 1–2 Start daily formula and definition drills
5 Mock week: a full set of papers in exam conditions A full set Mark everything; update the error log
4 Fix the mock: relearn every topic that lost marks, then amber topics 2 Finish a one-page summary for every topic
3 Timed papers from recent series 2–3 The redo cycle after every paper
2 Final mocks with the newest papers, in the order of your exams 2–3 Shift your sleep to fit the exam start times
1 Light review: summaries, flashcards, error-log rules; nothing new Parts of papers only Logistics: route, equipment, ID, statement of entry

The last two weeks

  • Follow the timetable. The subject you sit first gets the first mocks and the most review time in the final days.
  • Sit papers at exam times. If your papers start in the morning, do your mocks in the morning, so your brain is used to working hard at that hour.
  • Read your rules daily. Read the “rule for next time” column of your error log every day. It is a personal list of the traps you fall into.
  • Make one sheet per paper: the formulas, definitions and mistakes that matter most for that paper. Read it the evening before.
  • Plan the gaps between papers. With three days between two papers, for example: one timed paper on day 1, weak topics on day 2, light review on day 3.

Daily timetable templates

On a full revision day (study leave, weekends, or every day for a private candidate):

Time Activity
08:30–09:00 Flashcards and error-log rules
09:00–10:50 A timed paper (subject A)
10:50–11:10 Break, away from your desk
11:10–12:30 Mark the paper and log every lost mark
12:30–13:30 Lunch, away from screens
13:30–15:00 Relearn the topics the morning’s paper exposed
15:00–15:20 Break and some movement
15:20–16:50 Subject B: topic questions on a weak topic
16:50–19:00 Exercise, free time, dinner
19:00–20:00 Subject C: condensed notes and flashcards
From 20:00 Free time; screens off an hour before bed

That is about 7.5 hours of real work. More than this, day after day, usually means less is learned per hour.

On a school day, add about two hours after lessons:

Time Activity
17:00–17:45 Topic questions on a red or amber topic
18:00–18:45 One timed section of a past paper
19:45–20:30 Mark it, update the error log, 20 minutes of flashcards

Running your own mocks

If your school runs mock exams, treat them as the real thing. If you study alone, run your own:

  • the same length, the same time of day and the same rules as the real exam;
  • a clear table, no notes, phone in another room, and if possible someone in the room acting as the invigilator;
  • the whole set of papers over a few days, in the same order as your real timetable;
  • marking within 24 hours, followed by the redo cycle from Phase 4.

A disappointing mock is useful: it shows you the problems while there is still time to fix them. Treat the score as information, not as a judgement of you.

Condensing your notes

Condensing works because every step forces you to choose what matters and to recall it.

  1. Chapter notes from phase 2.
  2. One page per topic: write it from memory first, then check and fill the gaps.
  3. One page per paper: only the formulas, definitions and traps for that paper.
  4. A final card per paper to read on the evening before.

Formulas, definitions and data

Get a clean copy of what your board provides in the exam: for Cambridge, the formula list MF19 for Mathematics, the data and formulae pages printed in each Physics paper, and the Data Booklet for Chemistry. Learn what is on it, and where, so you never waste time searching. Then memorise everything else. Each day in the last three weeks, write out every formula and definition for one paper on a blank page in five minutes, check it, and correct it. Our sheets help: Maths, Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Business, economics and accounting.

Sleep, food and exercise

Your brain stores the day’s learning while you sleep, so sleep is part of revision, not time taken away from it. Most teenagers need 8–10 hours a night. An all-nighter before a paper makes you slower and more error-prone the next day. Two weeks before the exams, move your bedtime and wake-up time so that you are alert at the time your papers start. A daily walk or other exercise helps you sleep and manage stress, and avoiding caffeine after mid-afternoon protects your sleep. There is more in Motivation, sleep and stress.

What not to do

Don’t Do instead
Start new textbooks, courses or apps Stick to your notes, this guide and past papers
Reread your notes for hours Test yourself: papers, flashcards, blank pages
Revise only your favourite topics Work from your red and amber list
Sit papers without marking them Mark every paper within 24 hours
Use the newest papers too early Save them for the last three weeks
Stay up late to “finish” a topic Keep the same bedtime every night
Compare hours with friends or on social media Compare your scores with your own scores last week
TipRevise by question, not by chapter

In the final weeks, start from questions rather than from your notes. Do a question; if you cannot, open the chapter, fix that one gap, and try a similar question. Your time goes exactly where your marks are being lost.

Common mistakeThe last-week panic switch

In the final week, many students abandon their plan and start rereading everything from the beginning. It feels safe but achieves little, and it leaves no time for the subject you sit first. Trust the plan you made when you were calm: light review, error-log rules, sleep.

Exam techniqueTurn your mock into a timing plan

After each mock, note how long each question took. Then write a timing plan for each paper: for Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 (75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes), about 1.5 minutes per mark, so roughly 45 minutes for the first 30 marks. Practise the plan in your final mocks so that pacing feels automatic on the day.

Summary
  • Count back from your first paper; use the 8-week table, merging weeks if you have only six.
  • Weeks 8–6 for red topics, week 5 a full mock, week 4 fixing the mock, weeks 3–2 timed papers and final mocks, week 1 light review.
  • Sit papers at real exam times, mark within 24 hours, and read your error-log rules daily.
  • Condense: chapter notes, one page per topic, one page per paper, one card per paper.
  • Know what is on your formula list or data booklet, and memorise everything else.
  • Sleep 8–10 hours; shift your bedtime to the exam timetable two weeks ahead.
  • No new resources, no all-nighters, no last-week panic.

Preparation Roadmap/The road to exam day

Phase 6: Exam day, results and resits

GuideExamsAll subjects · all boardsStudy timeRead it a week before your first paper

Checklists for the night before and the morning of each exam; how to read the paper, manage your time and keep going when you are stuck; and what happens next: results day, enquiries about results, resits, UCAS Clearing and a plan B.

Why this matters

By exam day the learning is done, but marks can still be lost to things that have nothing to do with knowledge: a forgotten calculator, a misread question, fifteen minutes stuck on one part. This chapter removes those risks. It then walks you through what happens after the last paper, including what to do if results day does not go to plan.

The night before

  • Check the details on your statement of entry, the document from your centre that lists your candidate number and each paper’s date and start time. Confirm the time and the room, and set two alarms.
  • Pack your bag:
    • photo ID (a passport or national ID card): private candidates will not be allowed in without it;
    • your statement of entry;
    • a permitted calculator with fresh batteries;
    • at least three black pens, two pencils, an eraser, a sharpener and a ruler, plus a protractor and compasses for Mathematics;
    • a clear pencil case and a clear water bottle, if your centre allows them.
  • Check your calculator is allowed. Rules differ by board and subject. For example, Cambridge Mathematics does not allow graphic calculators or calculators that can do algebra.
  • Read your one-page sheet for the paper, then stop. Do not start anything new.
  • Plan your route, with time to spare for traffic, and go to bed at your normal time.
Common mistakePens, pencils and correction fluid

Cambridge papers ask for black or dark blue pen, and do not allow erasable pens or correction fluid. Use pencil only for diagrams and graphs, and for multiple-choice answer sheets, which are marked by machine and need a soft pencil. If you make a mistake in pen, cross it out with a single neat line and write the correction next to it.

The morning

  • Eat breakfast and drink some water, even if you are nervous.
  • Arrive at least 30 minutes early. Private candidates should check the arrival time their centre gives.
  • Take a last look at your one-page sheet, then put it away before you enter the room.
  • Leave your phone, smartwatch and any other device at home or hand them in as instructed. Having one with you in the exam room can count as malpractice, even if it is switched off.
  • Go to the toilet before the exam starts.

In the exam

Reading the paper

  1. Write your name, centre number and candidate number exactly as they appear on your statement of entry.
  2. Read the front cover: the number of questions, the total marks, and whether you must answer every question or choose some.
  3. If you have time, look through the whole paper for a minute so that nothing surprises you later.
  4. Read each question twice. Underline the command word and the key data.
  5. Look at the marks for each part and the space given for the answer. Both tell you how much the examiner expects.

Timing: minutes per mark

Divide the time by the total marks to get your pace. For example, Cambridge Mathematics Paper 1 has 75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes, which is about 1.5 minutes per mark, so a 6-mark question deserves about 9 minutes.

Cambridge paper Marks Time Minutes per mark
Mathematics Paper 1 or 3 75 1 h 50 min about 1.5
Mathematics Paper 2, 4, 5 or 6 50 1 h 15 min 1.5
Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 1 (multiple choice) 40 1 h 15 min just under 2 per question
Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 2 (AS structured) 60 1 h 15 min 1.25
Physics, Chemistry or Biology Paper 4 (A Level structured) 100 2 h 1.2
Business Paper 2 60 1 h 30 min 1.5
Economics Paper 2 60 2 h 2

To keep 10 minutes for checking in Mathematics Paper 1, work at about 1.3 minutes per mark. Edexcel IAL, AQA and OCR papers have different lengths, so work out your own pace from the front cover of a past paper.

Exam techniqueLet the marks guide you

The marks for each part tell you what the examiner wants. A 2-mark “explain” question usually needs two separate points, or one point and its reason. A 1-mark “state” question needs a short answer, not a paragraph. For calculations, a part worth 4 or 5 marks needs several clear steps of working, because most of those marks are method marks.

When you are stuck

  • Move on once you have spent about twice the time the marks deserve. Circle the question number and come back at the end.
  • Write what you know. A formula, a labelled diagram or the first line of working can earn method marks.
  • Use answers given in the question. If you cannot show that x=4 in part (a), use x=4 in part (b) anyway: the later marks are still available.
  • Never leave a multiple-choice question blank. No marks are taken away for wrong answers, so eliminate what you can and choose.
  • If panic starts, put your pen down, breathe slowly for thirty seconds, and read the next question. One hard question is only a few marks.
  • Need more space? Use the extra page at the back of the booklet, and write the question number clearly.

The last ten minutes

Check that you answered what was asked (“exact”, “in terms of π”, “to 3 significant figures”), that every answer has a unit where one is needed, that no part is left blank, and that your multiple-choice answer sheet is complete.

After each paper

Leave the room and do not go through the answers with friends: it only creates worry about marks you can no longer change. Eat, rest, then spend thirty minutes planning for your next paper. If something affected your performance, such as illness, a family emergency or a disturbance in the room, tell your exams officer the same day. Your centre may be able to apply for special consideration, but only within a short time after the exam.

Results day

  • When: Cambridge results for the May/June series come out in August (the June 2026 results were released on 11 August 2026), and results for the October/November series in January. Each Edexcel IAL series has its own results day; check Pearson’s key dates.
  • How: your centre gives you your results, and some centres also give you a login to see them online.
  • University places: if you applied through UCAS, check UCAS Hub on results day to see whether your place is confirmed. Before the exams, ask your centre whether it will send your results to UCAS.

Read your results calmly, and decide what to do before you phone anyone.

Enquiries about results

If a grade is lower than you expected, your centre can ask the board to check it. Cambridge calls these enquiries about results; Pearson, AQA and OCR call them post-results services or reviews of results. The usual options are:

  • a clerical re-check that all the marks were counted and added correctly;
  • a review of marking, with a faster priority service when a university place depends on the result;
  • a copy of your marked script, which shows exactly where you lost marks. This is very useful if you plan to resit.

Every service has a fee and a strict deadline, and it must be requested through your centre, including by private candidates. A review looks for marking errors; it is not a second marking, and marks can go down as well as up. It is usually worth it only if you believe you are close to a grade boundary.

Resits

Board When you can resit How it works
Cambridge International October/November (results in January), or the next May/June You normally sit all the papers of the AS or A Level again; ask your centre whether anything can be carried forward, such as an AS result within 13 months
Pearson Edexcel IAL January, May/June or October Modular: you can resit only the units you choose, and your best result for each unit counts
AQA and OCR (UK A Levels) May/June only Linear: you sit all the papers again, a year later

Resit when a university offer or a career depends on the grade, and when you know exactly what went wrong. If your university has already accepted you, the time is usually better spent preparing for the course. If you decide to resit, read the study planner example for a resit student, and start straight away.

TipWrite your plan B before results day

In July, while you are calm, write down what you will do if you miss your offer by one grade, and by two. On results day you will then follow a plan instead of making big decisions in a panic.

UCAS Clearing and plan B

If you miss the conditions of your offer, do not assume the worst. Universities sometimes accept students who just miss their grades, so check UCAS Hub first, and phone the admissions office if your status is unclear (have your UCAS Personal ID ready). If you have no place, Clearing lets you apply for university courses that still have places. You phone universities, and if one makes you an offer, you add it as your Clearing choice in UCAS Hub. Clearing is busiest on A Level results day and in the days after.

Other good plan B routes include:

  • a course with a foundation year, which has lower entry requirements;
  • a gap year with resits, then a new application with real grades instead of predicted ones;
  • universities in Turkey or other countries that accept A Level results;
  • apprenticeships and work-based routes.

There is more on applications in University applications and admissions tests.

Common mistakeDo not grab the first Clearing offer

An offer on the phone can feel like relief, but you will spend three or four years on that course. Ask about the course content, the city and the costs, compare two or three options, and talk it through with someone you trust before you accept.

Summary
  • Night before: statement of entry, photo ID, permitted calculator, black pens, pencils, eraser and ruler; normal bedtime.
  • Morning: breakfast, arrive at least 30 minutes early, no phone or smartwatch in the room.
  • Pace yourself by minutes per mark: about 1.5 in Cambridge Maths Paper 1 (75 marks in 1 hour 50 minutes).
  • Stuck? Move on, write what you know, use given answers, never leave a multiple-choice question blank.
  • Report illness or disruption to your exams officer the same day.
  • Cambridge June results come out in August, November results in January. Enquiries about results have fees and short deadlines, and marks can go down.
  • Resits: Cambridge in November or June, Edexcel IAL in January, June or October (best unit result counts), AQA and OCR in June only.
  • Write a plan B before results day; Clearing, foundation years and gap years are all good routes.

You have reached the end of the road. Go back to The preparation road at a glance at any time to check where you are, or read Studying as a private candidate if you are preparing without a school.

PreviousPhase 5: Final revisionNextStudy methods that actually work
Preparation Roadmap/Skills that raise grades

Study methods that actually work

GuideExamsAll boards · all subjectsStudy time45 minutes to read, then use all year

Research shows that some popular study habits, such as rereading and highlighting, do very little. This chapter shows you the methods that do work (testing yourself, spacing and mixing your practice) and how to build them into a normal week.

Why this matters

Two students can study for the same hours and get very different grades. Usually the difference is method, not talent. Rereading feels productive but builds familiarity, not memory. Testing yourself feels harder, and that difficulty is what makes knowledge stay. Change how you study and every hour from now on is worth more.

Before you start, read The preparation road at a glance so you know where these methods fit. They are the engine of Phase 2: Learn the content and Phase 3: Practise and test yourself.

What the research says

In 2013 the psychologist John Dunlosky and four colleagues reviewed the research on ten popular learning techniques and rated how useful each one is for real students.

Rating Technique What it means
High Practice testing Recalling or answering questions without looking
High Distributed practice Spreading study of a topic over days or weeks
Moderate Elaborative interrogation Asking yourself “why is this true?”
Moderate Self-explanation Explaining each step of a solution to yourself
Moderate Interleaved practice Mixing problem types in one session
Low Summarising Writing shorter versions of a text
Low Highlighting Marking key words while reading
Low Keyword mnemonics Linking new words to memorable images
Low Imagery for text Picturing what you read
Low Rereading Reading the same notes again

“Low” does not mean useless; it means a small benefit for the time it takes. Yet rereading and highlighting are the most popular study habits of all. They feel good because familiar words make your brain mistake “I recognise this” for “I know this”, an illusion of competence. The exam gives you a blank space, not the page, so producing knowledge from memory is what you must practise.

Retrieval practice: test yourself first

Retrieval practice

Learning by recalling information from memory (for example by answering questions or writing everything you remember on a topic) instead of rereading it. Each successful recall makes the memory stronger and easier to find later.

Retrieval works even when you get answers wrong, as long as you check and correct them straight away. Good ways to retrieve:

  • Blank-page recall (“blurting”). Close your notes and write everything you remember about a topic for 10 minutes. Then fill the gaps from your notes in a different colour. The coloured parts are your revision list.
  • Chapter questions. Do the practice questions at the end of each chapter here without looking back.
  • Flashcards (see below) and past-paper questions, which are retrieval in the exact form the exam uses. See Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes.
TipTurn your notes into questions

After you finish a section, write three questions it answers in the margin, for example “What does the discriminant tell you?” Next time, cover the notes and answer the questions. Your notes become a self-test instead of something to reread.

Spacing: little and often beats one long session

Spaced practice

Spreading study of the same material over several sessions separated by gaps of days or weeks, instead of doing it all at once. Also called distributed practice.

Memory fades quickly after you first learn something, and each recall after a gap makes it fade more slowly. A useful rule of thumb is to review a new topic about 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and 1 month after first learning it. The exact gaps matter less than the habit of coming back.

The opposite is cramming: everything in one long session just before a test. It can get you through tomorrow’s test, but most of it is gone weeks later, and A Levels examine two years of content at the end.

Common mistakeRewatching is rereading

Watching the same video lesson twice is the video version of rereading. Watch it once, carefully, then close it and test yourself. Rewatch only the part you could not recall.

Interleaving: mix your practice

Interleaving

Mixing different topics or types of problem within one practice session (for example differentiation, vectors and probability), so that you must decide which method each question needs.

When you do twenty questions on one method in a row (blocked practice), you know the method before you read the question. In the exam, nobody tells you, and interleaving trains that choice. Use blocked practice for a brand-new topic, then switch to mixed sets once the basic questions feel easy.

Making ideas stick: elaboration, examples and pictures

Elaboration means connecting a new idea to what you already know by asking “why?” and “how?”. Why does a higher temperature speed up a reaction? How does that link to activation energy? Every connection is another route your memory can use.

Concrete examples make abstract ideas easy to picture. “Price elastic demand” is hard to remember; “when one brand of crisps raises its price, many buyers switch brands” is easy. Collect one or two examples of your own for every definition.

Dual coding means combining words with visuals. Draw blood flow through the heart, a supply and demand diagram or a flowchart of protein synthesis, and label it from memory. Words and pictures give you two routes to the same idea.

Worked examples, then fade them

When you are a beginner, solving problems alone can overload you, so study a worked example first. Then remove the support step by step:

Stage What you do
1. Study Read a full worked example. Explain each step to yourself: why this step, why now?
2. Complete Try a similar example where the last steps are hidden. Finish it.
3. Solo Do a similar question with no help, then check against a full solution.
4. Mixed Do the same type of question inside a mixed set, under time pressure.

Once you reach stage 4 easily, stop studying examples for that topic and spend your time on questions.

The Feynman technique

The physicist Richard Feynman was famous for explaining hard ideas in simple words. This technique finds exactly where your understanding breaks.

  1. Choose one concept, for example “moles” or “opportunity cost”.
  2. Explain it out loud or on paper as if teaching a younger student. Use plain words and an example.
  3. Notice where you hesitate, use jargon you cannot explain, or say “it just is”. Those are your gaps.
  4. Go back to your notes or the chapter and fix those gaps only.
  5. Explain it again, more simply. Finish with the exact syllabus definition.
TipIf English is your second language

Explain the idea first in your own language to check you understand it. Then explain it again in English, using the precise syllabus terms. Examiners reward the correct technical words, so collect them in a personal word list with a short meaning next to each.

Spaced-repetition flashcards

Flashcards combine retrieval and spacing. A spaced-repetition app such as Anki (free on computers, Android and the web) shows each card just before you are likely to forget it: cards you know appear rarely, and cards you miss come back soon.

  • One fact per card. “State the units of the Planck constant” is a good card; “quantum physics” is not.
  • Make your own cards. Writing them is learning, and shared decks often do not match your syllabus.
  • Use cards for exact facts: definitions, equations, units, reagents and conditions. Use diagrams and questions for processes and problem-solving.
  • Review every day, and add only about 10 to 20 new cards a day so reviews do not pile up.

On paper, use the Leitner system: review box 1 daily, box 2 every three days and box 3 weekly. A correct card moves up a box; a wrong card goes back to box 1.

Focus: your phone is the biggest problem

Every time you check a message, it takes minutes to regain full concentration, and a phone on the desk distracts you even when it is silent.

  • Put the phone in another room, or use a focus mode that blocks apps while you study.
  • Choose one specific task before you start: “Questions 1 to 6 on the discriminant”, not “do maths”.
  • Study at the same place and time when you can. Routine makes starting easier.

The Pomodoro technique makes this easy: 25 minutes of full focus, then a 5-minute break; after four rounds, a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. Try it now with the timer below: pick one task, press start, and do not touch your phone until it rings. As your focus grows, you can stretch the blocks to 40 or 50 minutes.

Maths and science versus essay subjects

The same principles apply everywhere, but what you practise is different.

Subject type Main thing to practise Best retrieval tool Typical trap
Mathematics Many questions, in mixed sets Questions with worked answers Reading solutions before trying
Physics and Chemistry Definitions, equations, calculations, practical skills Flashcards; past-paper questions Learning calculations but not explanations
Biology Precise terms, processes, data analysis Diagrams from memory; long answers Vague words such as “it affects”
Business and Economics Definitions, diagrams, evaluation Timed paragraph plans; case studies Describing the case instead of analysing it

For essay subjects, write full answers regularly and compare them with the mark scheme’s levels; see Writing top-band business answers.

Studying with friends

Group study works when everyone tests and explains, and fails when it turns into chatting. Keep groups to two to four people, agree a topic and a finishing time, and use the time to quiz each other, take turns teaching a topic (the Feynman technique with a real audience), mark each other’s answers with the official mark scheme, or compare essay plans. If you study alone as a private candidate, an online study partner gives the same benefits.

Using AI tools responsibly

AI chat tools can be excellent tutors or terrible ones. The rule: use AI to explain and to check, never to do the practice for you. Learning happens when your own brain retrieves and works things out. If a tool does that work, you get none of the benefit, and you still meet the exam alone.

Good uses Bad uses
“Explain the discriminant in a different way, with an example.” “Solve these ten homework questions for me.”
“Here is my answer and the mark scheme. Which marks did I miss?” Copying an AI answer into your notes without trying first
“Quiz me on Group 2 trends, one question at a time.” Trusting AI calculations or facts without checking
“Translate this sentence from the question into simpler English.” Submitting AI-written work in coursework or applications
Common mistakeAI can be confidently wrong

AI tools sometimes give wrong facts, wrong numbers or answers for a different syllabus, in a confident tone. Check against your syllabus, a trusted textbook or the mark scheme. In coursework or non-exam assessment, presenting AI-generated work as your own is malpractice and can lead to disqualification.

A sample weekly schedule

Here is a realistic week for a student taking Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry, with about two hours of independent study on weekdays. Each block is two Pomodoros (about 50 minutes). Swap in your own subjects; the structure is what matters. For a plan built around your exam dates, use Build your personal study plan.

Day Block 1 Block 2 Short review (15 min)
Monday Maths: learn a new topic Physics: questions on last week’s topic Flashcards
Tuesday Chemistry: learn a new topic Maths: questions on Monday’s topic Flashcards + blank-page recall of Monday’s maths
Wednesday Physics: learn a new topic Chemistry: questions on Tuesday’s topic Flashcards
Thursday Maths: mixed question set Physics: questions on Wednesday’s topic Flashcards + update error log
Friday Chemistry: mixed question set Maths: redo last week’s wrong questions Flashcards
Saturday One timed past-paper section (rotate the subject each week) Mark it with the mark scheme Add mistakes to error log
Sunday Rest Plan next week (10 minutes) Optional light flashcards

Each subject returns several times (spacing), new content is tested on a later day (retrieval), Thursday and Friday mix topics (interleaving), and Saturday is a test. Sunday’s rest protects your motivation; see Motivation, sleep and stress.

Quick check
Summary
  • Test yourself instead of rereading: retrieval practice and spaced practice were the two techniques rated high utility in the 2013 review.
  • Review new topics after gaps of about 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and 1 month. Avoid cramming.
  • Learn new methods with blocked practice, then switch to mixed (interleaved) question sets.
  • Connect ideas by asking “why?”, collect concrete examples, and draw diagrams from memory.
  • Study worked examples first, then fade the support until you can solve questions alone.
  • Use flashcards with spaced repetition (such as Anki) for facts that must be exact.
  • Put your phone in another room and work in focused blocks such as 25-minute Pomodoros.
  • Use AI to explain and check, never to do your practice or your coursework.

Next: Exam technique shows how to turn what you know into marks.

PreviousPhase 6: Exam day, results and resitsNextExam technique
Preparation Roadmap/Skills that raise grades

Exam technique

GuideExamsAll boards · all subjectsStudy time1 hour to read, then practise with every past paper

Knowing the content is half the job; the other half is turning it into marks. This chapter covers reading questions, timing, working, accuracy and units, and how to answer every type of question, from multiple choice to essays and practical papers.

Why this matters

Examiners can only mark what is on the page. Every year, examiner reports repeat the same message: many candidates lose marks they could have earned by misreading the question, leaving out units, rounding too early or running out of time. These are skills, and skills can be practised. The habits in this chapter are worth a grade or more to many students.

Before you start, it helps to know what each instruction word means: see Command words decoded. Practise every habit here with real papers, as described in Phase 4: Past papers and mark schemes.

Read the question, then read it again

Most lost marks start in the first ten seconds, when a student sees a familiar topic and starts writing the answer to a question they expected, not the one printed. Use the same routine for every question:

  1. Read the whole question, including any introduction, data or diagram. Information is there because you need it.
  2. Underline the command word (describe, explain, calculate, evaluate…) and the topic.
  3. Circle any conditions: “two reasons”, “exact”, “to 3 significant figures”, “with reference to the data”, “using your answer to (a)”.
  4. Look at the marks and plan that many separate points.
  5. Answer, then reread the question to check you answered what was asked.

Marks tell you how much to write and how long to spend

As a rough guide, one mark needs one correct, separate point. A 3-mark “explain” question needs three linked steps of reasoning, not one long sentence. The number of answer lines is a second clue: if you have filled two lines for a 6-mark question, you have probably missed something.

Marks also set your time budget. Divide the time by the total marks:

Cambridge paper Time Marks Time per mark
Mathematics 9709 Paper 1 or 3 1 h 50 min 75 about 1.5 min
Mathematics 9709 Paper 4, 5 or 6 1 h 15 min 50 1.5 min
Sciences Paper 1 (multiple choice) 1 h 15 min 40 questions about 1 min 50 s per question
Sciences Paper 2 (AS structured) 1 h 15 min 60 1.25 min
Sciences Paper 4 (A Level structured) 2 h 100 1.2 min
Business 9609 Paper 2 1 h 30 min 60 1.5 min
Economics 9708 Paper 2 2 h 60 2 min

So an 8-mark maths question deserves about 12 minutes. If you have spent 20, move on and come back later.

TipWrite checkpoints on the front page

At the start, write two or three checkpoint times, for example “halfway marks by 10:00”. A quick glance at the clock then tells you whether you are on pace, without constant calculation.

Show your working

In mathematics and in science calculations, many marks are for method. In mark schemes, M marks are for a correct method, A marks are for accuracy and depend on the method mark, and B marks are independent. If your final answer is wrong but your method is visible, you can still earn many of the marks. A bare wrong answer earns nothing.

Examiners also use error carried forward (often called “follow through”): if you make a mistake in part (a) and then use your wrong answer correctly in part (b), you can usually still earn the part (b) marks. That only works if they can see what you did.

Use the same pattern every time: formula, substitution, answer with unit.

Ek=12mv2=12×0.50×4.02=4.0 J
Exam technique“Show that” questions

When the answer is printed in the question, the marks are for the route, not the result. Every step must be visible, with no jumps. Then use the given result in the next part, even if you could not prove it: the later marks are still available.

Significant figures, units and rounding

  • Do not round in the middle of a calculation. Keep the full value on your calculator (use the memory or ANS key) and round only the final answer.
  • Mathematics: give answers to 3 significant figures unless told otherwise, and angles in degrees to 1 decimal place. If the question says exact, leave answers as surds, fractions or in terms of π or ln⁡.
  • Sciences: give the final answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data, usually 2 or 3. Never fewer.
  • Units: write a unit on every final answer and check the prefix. A missing or wrong unit often costs a mark on its own.
Common mistakeEarly rounding changes the answer

A ball of mass 0.65 kg falls 1.8 m from rest. Take g=9.81 m s−2. Its speed is v=2×9.81×1.8=5.9427… m s−1. If you round v to 5.9 and then calculate 12mv2, you get 11.3 J. Keeping the full value gives 11.5 J, which matches mgh=0.65×9.81×1.8. One early rounding lost the accuracy mark.

Multiple choice

Cambridge science Paper 1 has 40 questions in 1 hour 15 minutes: about 1 minute 50 seconds each. Economics Papers 1 and 3 are also multiple choice. Edexcel IAL and the UK boards mix multiple-choice questions into some written papers instead.

  • Answer before you look. Cover the options, work out your answer, then find it. This protects you from attractive wrong options.
  • Eliminate. Cross out options you know are wrong. With two options left, even a guess has a 50% chance.
  • Watch for NOT, FALSE and INCORRECT, usually in bold. Underline them.
  • Check powers of ten and units. Wrong options are often your answer with a factor of 10, 1000 or 2 missing.
  • Never leave a blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so guess any question you cannot do.
  • Transfer carefully. If the paper uses a separate answer sheet, check every answer is on the correct line.

Structured questions

Structured questions are split into parts: (a), (b)(i), (b)(ii). They usually build on each other, so an answer to (a) is often a hint for (b). Keep answers precise: use the technical term, give one idea per mark, and do not copy out the question. “With reference to the data” or “use the information” means quote figures from the question, with units, in your answer.

Extended writing

For long answers in any subject, build each paragraph with Point, Evidence, Explain: make one clear point, support it with evidence or data, and explain why it matters to the question.

In Business and Economics, the mark scheme rewards four skills in order: knowledge (correct terms and theory), application (using the business or economy in the case), analysis (chains of reasoning: “this means that… so…”) and evaluation (a supported judgement). The top levels require evaluation, so a long, accurate answer with no judgement cannot reach full marks. See Writing top-band business answers.

Data, graphs and diagrams

When you describe data, give the overall trend, quote key values with units, describe any change in the rate of change, and point out anomalies. “Sales rose from 1200 to 1800 units, an increase of 50%” earns more than “sales went up”.

When you draw a graph:

  • label both axes with quantity and unit, for example “time / s”;
  • choose a scale so that the points cover at least half the grid in each direction;
  • plot points with small, precise crosses;
  • draw a single best-fit line or smooth curve, never dot-to-dot;
  • find a gradient using a large triangle, and show the values you read.

In Business and Economics diagrams, label the axes (price, quantity), every curve (D₁, D₂, S), the equilibrium points, and show shifts with arrows. Then refer to the diagram in your writing.

Practical and planning papers (Cambridge Papers 3 and 5)

Cambridge Physics, Chemistry and Biology each have two practical-skills papers.

Paper 3: Advanced Practical Skills (AS) Paper 5: Planning, Analysis and Evaluation (A Level)
Format 2 h, 40 marks, hands-on in a laboratory 1 h 15 min, 30 marks, written
What you do Follow instructions, take measurements, record, graph, calculate Plan an experiment, analyse given data, evaluate conclusions
Key marks Tables with “quantity / unit” headings; readings to the precision of the instrument; repeats; good graphs; specific improvements Clear variables (independent, dependent, controlled); a workable method; safety; how to analyse (what to plot); uncertainties and error bars

In Paper 3, improvements must be specific: “use a video camera with a timer to measure the oscillation time” earns marks, “be more careful” never does. Edexcel IAL tests practical skills in written papers instead (Units 3 and 6). The subject guides go further: Physics practical skills, Chemistry practical skills and Biology practical skills.

Checking and getting unstuck

Leave about 5 to 10 minutes at the end. Check that every question has an answer, every final answer has a unit and the right significant figures, and that each answer matches its command word. Ask “is this sensible?”: a car is not travelling at 3000 m s−1.

When you are stuck:

  • Mark the question, move on, and come back with fresh eyes.
  • Write what you know: the relevant formula, a definition, a labelled diagram. These can earn marks on their own.
  • Use every piece of given information; if you have not used something, that is probably the key.
  • Write inside the answer space. If you need more room, use the extra page provided and label the question number clearly.

Common ways marks are lost

Mistake Fix
Describing when asked to explain Underline the command word before writing
Missing or wrong units Write the unit with every final answer
Rounding too early Keep full values; round only at the end
Bare answers with no working Formula, substitution, answer
Vague words such as “it affects” State the direction and size of the change
Ignoring the context in a case study Use the business’s name and its data
One-sided evaluation Weigh both sides, then make a justified judgement
Running out of time Use your time per mark and checkpoints

Weak and strong answers compared

A science “explain” question. Explain why the rate of a reaction increases when the temperature is increased. [3 marks]

Weak answer (about 1 mark)

The particles move faster, so they collide more and the reaction goes faster.

This repeats the question (“goes faster”) and never mentions activation energy or successful collisions.

Strong answer (3 marks)

At a higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy. [B1] So a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. [B1] Therefore the frequency of successful collisions increases. [B1]

A business “evaluate” question. Leyla’s Bakery made a net profit of $18,000 last year. Leyla needs $40,000 to open a second shop. Evaluate whether she should finance it with a bank loan. [12 marks]

Weak paragraph

A bank loan is good because you get money quickly and do not lose control. But you have to pay interest. Overall she should take the loan.

Correct knowledge, but nothing about Leyla’s bakery, no chain of reasoning, and a judgement with no reason.

Strong paragraph

A loan lets Leyla keep full ownership and control (knowledge). Her $18,000 profit suggests she could afford repayments from current earnings (application). However, a new shop may take months to build sales, while repayments are fixed, so cash flow could turn negative and put both shops at risk (analysis). A loan is the better choice only if her forecast for the new shop is realistic and she keeps a cash reserve; if sales are uncertain, a partner sharing the risk may be safer (evaluation).

The strong paragraph is not much longer. It earns more because every sentence does a job: it uses the case, builds a chain of reasoning and ends with a judgement that depends on clear conditions.

Quick check
Summary
  • Underline the command word and topic, circle conditions, and check the marks before you write.
  • One mark is roughly one separate point. Use time per mark (for example about 1.5 minutes per mark in Cambridge Maths Paper 1) and move on if a question overruns.
  • Show formula, substitution and answer. Method marks and follow-through marks reward visible working.
  • Round only at the end: 3 significant figures in maths unless told otherwise; match the data in science. Always give units.
  • In multiple choice, answer before looking at the options, eliminate, and never leave a blank.
  • For extended writing, build point, evidence, explain paragraphs; in Business and Economics show knowledge, application, analysis and a justified judgement.
  • In practical papers, use “quantity / unit” headings, good graph technique and specific improvements.
