Mathematics/Pure Mathematics 1

Quadratics

AS LevelExamsCAIE P1 · Edexcel IAL P1 · AQA/OCR/Edexcel PureStudy time6–8 hours

A quadratic is any expression whose highest power of x is x2. You will learn to solve quadratic equations in three ways, read their graphs, count their solutions without solving, and handle quadratic inequalities and simultaneous equations.

Why this matters

Quadratics are the first topic in Paper 1 and they come back everywhere: in coordinate geometry, functions, calculus, mechanics and physics. A ball thrown in the air, the area of a field, the profit of a business at different prices: all of these are modelled by quadratics. If this chapter feels solid, a large part of A Level Pure Mathematics becomes easier.

Before you start, you should be comfortable with Algebra from scratch (expanding brackets, factorising, rearranging) and with Powers, roots, surds and standard form.

What is a quadratic?

Start with an expression you already know, like 3x+5. The highest power of x is x1, so we call it linear: its graph is a straight line. Now allow an x2 term, for example x2−2x−3. The graph is no longer straight. It bends into a symmetrical U-shape called a parabola, and the expression is called a quadratic.

Quadratic expression

An expression that can be written in the form ax2+bx+c, where a, b and c are constants and a≠0.

The numbers a, b and c are called coefficients. In 2x2−7x+3 we have a=2, b=−7 and c=3. Notice that the sign belongs to the number: b is −7, not 7. Getting this wrong is the most common way to lose marks later in this chapter.

Coefficient

The number multiplying a power of the variable. In ax2+bx+c, a is the coefficient of x2, b is the coefficient of x, and c is the constant term.

A quadratic equation sets a quadratic equal to zero, such as x2−2x−3=0. Its solutions are called roots. Most quadratic equations have two roots, some have one, and some have no real roots at all. By the end of this chapter you will be able to predict which, before solving anything.

Root (of an equation)

A value of the variable that makes the equation true. The real roots of f(x)=0 are the x-coordinates where the graph of y=f(x) meets the x-axis.

The shape of a quadratic graph

Every quadratic graph is a parabola, and four facts let you sketch one quickly.

  1. Which way up? If a>0 the graph is ∪-shaped (it has a lowest point). If a<0 it is ∩-shaped (it has a highest point).
  2. Where does it cross the y-axis? Put x=0: you get y=c. So the y-intercept is (0,c).
  3. Where does it cross the x-axis? At the roots of ax2+bx+c=0, if there are any.
  4. Where is the turning point? The lowest or highest point is called the vertex. The graph is symmetrical about a vertical line through the vertex, called the line of symmetry.
Think of it like this

Think of the parabola as a bowl. Water poured into a ∪-shaped bowl collects at the bottom, which is the vertex. The two roots are where the rim of the bowl crosses the table top (the x-axis). If the whole bowl sits above the table, there are no crossing points, so there are no real roots.

Use the sliders below to change a, b and c and watch what happens. Make a negative and the bowl flips. Change c and the whole graph slides up or down. Notice what happens to the roots as the vertex rises above the x-axis.

Method 1: solving by factorising

Factorising works because of one simple fact.

Key factsThe zero product rule

If A×B=0, then A=0 or B=0 (or both).

So if we can write a quadratic as two brackets multiplied together, each bracket gives us one root.

When a=1

To factorise x2+bx+c, look for two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b.

Worked exampleSolve x2−5x+6=0

We need two numbers that multiply to +6 and add to −5. Try the factor pairs of 6: (1,6), (2,3), (−1,−6), (−2,−3). Only −2 and −3 add to −5.

x2−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3)=0

So x−2=0 or x−3=0, giving x=2 or x=3.

Check: 22−5(2)+6=4−10+6=0. It works.

When a≠1: the “ac method”

Multiply a by c. Find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b. Use them to split the middle term, then factorise in pairs.

Worked exampleSolve 2x2+7x−4=0

Here ac=2×(−4)=−8. Two numbers that multiply to −8 and add to 7 are 8 and −1.

Split the middle term: 2x2+8x−x−4=0

Factorise in pairs: 2x(x+4)−1(x+4)=0

Take out the common bracket: (2x−1)(x+4)=0

So x=12 or x=−4.

Common mistakeNever divide by x

To solve x2=3x, it is tempting to divide both sides by x and get x=3. But this loses a solution, because x might be zero (and you cannot divide by zero). Instead, rearrange to x2−3x=0, factorise to x(x−3)=0, and get both answers: x=0 or x=3.

Factorising is the quickest method when it works. It only works neatly when the roots are rational (whole numbers or fractions). If you cannot find the two numbers within about a minute, switch to one of the next two methods.

Method 2: completing the square

Completing the square rewrites a quadratic so you can see its vertex immediately. Exam questions often say “express in the form a(x+p)2+q” or “(x−p)2+q”. That is a request to complete the square.

The idea comes from expanding a squared bracket:

(x+3)2=x2+6x+9

So x2+6x is “nearly” (x+3)2. It is just missing the 9:

x2+6x=(x+3)2−9
Key factsCompleting the square (when a=1)

x2+bx=(x+b2)2−(b2)2 Halve the coefficient of x to get the number in the bracket, then subtract that number squared.

Worked exampleWrite x2+6x+11 in the form (x+p)2+q. Hence state the minimum point.

Half of 6 is 3, so

x2+6x+11=(x+3)2−9+11=(x+3)2+2

A square is never negative, so (x+3)2≥0. The smallest value of the whole expression is 0+2=2, and this happens when x+3=0, that is x=−3.

The minimum point of y=x2+6x+11 is (−3,2).

TipReading the vertex from completed square form

For y=a(x+p)2+q, the vertex is at (−p,q). Watch the sign: (x−4)2 gives x=+4, while (x+4)2 gives x=−4.

When a≠1

Take a out as a factor of the x2 and x terms first, complete the square inside the bracket, then multiply back out.

Worked exampleExpress 2x2−12x+7 in the form a(x+b)2+c. Hence state the coordinates of the vertex of y=2x2−12x+7 and the range of f(x)=2x2−12x+7.

Factor 2 out of the first two terms: 2x2−12x+7=2(x2−6x)+7 Complete the square inside the bracket: x2−6x=(x−3)2−9. M1 =2[(x−3)2−9]+7=2(x−3)2−18+7 =2(x−3)2−11 A1

So a=2, b=−3, c=−11.

The vertex is at (3,−11). B1 Because a=2>0, this is a minimum, so the range is f(x)≥−11. B1

Check: put x=0 into both forms. 2(0)2−12(0)+7=7 and 2(0−3)2−11=18−11=7. They match.

You can also solve equations by completing the square: rewrite the equation, then take square roots. Remember that taking a square root gives two answers, positive and negative.

Worked exampleSolve x2+4x−1=0, giving exact answers.

(x+2)2−4−1=0⇒(x+2)2=5 x+2=±5⇒x=−2±5 “Exact” means leave the surd in. As decimals these are 0.236 and −4.24 (3 s.f.).

Method 3: the quadratic formula

If you complete the square on the general quadratic ax2+bx+c=0, you get a formula that solves every quadratic equation.

Key factsThe quadratic formula

The solutions of ax2+bx+c=0 are x=−b±b2−4ac2a

Worked exampleSolve 3x2−4x−2=0, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.

Identify the coefficients carefully, signs included: a=3, b=−4, c=−2. x=−(−4)±(−4)2−4(3)(−2)2(3)=4±16+246=4±406 M1 x=1.72orx=−0.387 A1

Common mistakeSign slips in the formula

Two errors cost more marks than any others: writing −b as −4 when b=−4 (it should be +4), and squaring a negative b wrongly. (−4)2=16, but if you type −42 into a calculator you get −16. Always use brackets: (−4)2.

Exam techniqueWhich method should I use?

If the question says “factorise”, “complete the square” or “express in the form…”, you must use that method. Otherwise, try factorising first; if it does not work quickly, use the formula. If the question asks for exact answers, keep surds such as 5. If it asks for 3 significant figures, give exactly three. Cambridge examiners deduct for wrong accuracy.

The discriminant: how many roots?

Look again at the quadratic formula. The part under the square root, b2−4ac, decides everything:

  • If it is positive, ±x gives two different answers, so there are two distinct real roots.
  • If it is zero, ±0 adds and subtracts nothing, so there is one repeated root (often called “equal roots”).
  • If it is negative, there is no real square root, so there are no real roots.
Discriminant

The quantity b2−4ac for the quadratic ax2+bx+c. Its sign tells you how many real roots the equation ax2+bx+c=0 has.

Worked exampleFind the values of k for which x2+kx+9=0 has equal roots.

Equal roots means the discriminant is zero: a=1, b=k, c=9. k2−4(1)(9)=0⇒k2=36⇒k=±6 Check: with k=6, x2+6x+9=(x+3)2, which does have a repeated root.

Lines meeting curves

A favourite Paper 1 question asks when a straight line meets, touches (is a tangent to), or misses a curve. The method is always the same: set the two equations equal, rearrange into a quadratic equal to zero, and look at its discriminant.

The line… Number of meeting points Discriminant
cuts the curve 2 b2−4ac>0
touches the curve (tangent) 1 b2−4ac=0
misses the curve 0 b2−4ac<0
Worked exampleFind the set of values of k for which the line y=kx−1 intersects the curve y=x2+3 at two distinct points.

At intersection the y-values are equal: x2+3=kx−1⇒x2−kx+4=0 M1 Two distinct points means two distinct roots, so the discriminant is positive: (−k)2−4(1)(4)>0⇒k2>16 M1 k2>16 when k>4 or k<−4 (see inequalities below). A1

Quadratic inequalities

To solve x2−x−12>0 you need all the values of x that make the quadratic positive, not just a couple of numbers. The reliable method has three steps.

  1. Solve the equation x2−x−12=0 to find the critical values. Here (x−4)(x+3)=0, so x=4 or x=−3.
  2. Sketch the graph. a=1>0, so it is ∪-shaped, crossing the x-axis at −3 and 4.
  3. Read off the answer. “>0” means “where is the graph above the x-axis?” That is to the left of −3 and to the right of 4: x<−3 or x>4.

If the question had been x2−x−12<0 (below the axis), the answer would be the part in the middle: −3<x<4.

Worked exampleSolve 2x2+5x−3≤0.

Factorise: (2x−1)(x+3)=0 gives critical values x=12 and x=−3. M1

The graph is ∪-shaped, and “≤0” means on or below the axis, which is between the roots. The end points are included because of the “=” in ≤: −3≤x≤12 A1

Common mistakeTwo inequalities cannot be squashed together the wrong way

For “x<−3 or x>4” never write −3>x>4. That would mean x is less than −3 and greater than 4 at the same time, which is impossible. Write two separate inequalities joined by “or”. A combined form like −3<x<4 is only correct for the region between the roots.

Simultaneous equations: one linear, one quadratic

When one equation is linear and the other is quadratic, use substitution: rearrange the linear equation to make one letter the subject, then substitute into the quadratic.

Worked exampleSolve the simultaneous equations y=x+1 and x2+y2=25.

Substitute y=x+1 into the second equation: x2+(x+1)2=25⇒2x2+2x+1−25=0⇒x2+x−12=0 M1 (x+4)(x−3)=0⇒x=−4 or x=3 A1 Now find each y from the linear equation: x=−4⇒y=−3, and x=3⇒y=4. A1

Solutions: (−4,−3) and (3,4). Geometrically, these are the two points where the line crosses the circle of radius 5.

TipPair your answers

Always present the answers as pairs, (x,y). An examiner cannot give the final mark for “x=−4,3 and y=−3,4” if it is unclear which y goes with which x.

Disguised quadratics

Some equations are quadratics in disguise. If an equation contains a quantity and its square, such as x2 and x4, or x and x, substitute a new letter.

Worked exampleSolve x4−5x2+4=0.

Let u=x2. Then x4=u2, and the equation becomes u2−5u+4=0⇒(u−1)(u−4)=0⇒u=1 or u=4 Go back to x: x2=1 gives x=±1, and x2=4 gives x=±2. There are four solutions: x=−2,−1,1,2.

Worked exampleSolve 2x−7x+3=0.

Let u=x, so x=u2: 2u2−7u+3=0⇒(2u−1)(u−3)=0⇒u=12 or u=3 Then x=u2, so x=14 or x=9. Because x can never be negative, any negative value of u would have to be rejected. Here both are positive, so both answers stand.

Board differences

All boards teach the same quadratics content in their first Pure paper (Cambridge P1, Edexcel IAL P1, and Year 1 Pure for AQA, OCR and Edexcel in the UK). The UK boards also expect you to use the discriminant inside proof questions (“prove that the equation has no real roots for all values of k”). Cambridge mostly tests it through line-and-curve intersections and the range of a function.

Try it yourselfStart easy, finish at exam standard

  1. Solve x2+7x+10=0 by factorising.

    Show answer

    Two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7 are 2 and 5. (x+2)(x+5)=0, so x=−2 or x=−5.

  2. Solve 3x2−10x−8=0 by factorising.

    Show answer

    ac=−24. Two numbers that multiply to −24 and add to −10 are −12 and 2. 3x2−12x+2x−8=3x(x−4)+2(x−4)=(3x+2)(x−4), so x=−23 or x=4.

  3. Express x2−8x+3 in the form (x+p)2+q and state the coordinates of the minimum point of y=x2−8x+3.

    Show answer

    Half of −8 is −4: x2−8x+3=(x−4)2−16+3=(x−4)2−13. The minimum point is (4,−13).

  4. Solve 5x2+2x−1=0, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.

    Show answer

    x=−2±4+2010=−2±2410, so x=0.290 or x=−0.690.

  5. Find the set of values of k for which kx2+4x+k=0 has no real roots.

    Show answer

    No real roots means b2−4ac<0: 16−4k2<0, so k2>4, giving k<−2 or k>2.

  6. Solve the inequality x2+2x−15<0.

    Show answer

    (x+5)(x−3)=0 gives critical values −5 and 3. The graph is ∪-shaped and we want the part below the axis: −5<x<3.

  7. Solve the simultaneous equations y=2x−1 and y=x2−4x+4.

    Show answer

    x2−4x+4=2x−1⇒x2−6x+5=0⇒(x−1)(x−5)=0. M1 x=1⇒y=1 and x=5⇒y=9. Solutions (1,1) and (5,9). [A1 A1]

  8. (Exam style) f(x)=−x2+6x−5. (a) Express f(x) in the form a−(x−b)2. (b) State the maximum value of f(x) and the value of x at which it occurs. (c) Find the set of values of k for which the line y=k meets the curve y=f(x) at two distinct points.

    Show answer

    (a) −x2+6x−5=−(x2−6x)−5=−[(x−3)2−9]−5=4−(x−3)2. [M1 A1] (b) A square is never negative, so the largest value is 4, when x=3. B1 (c) The horizontal line y=k cuts the ∩-shaped curve twice when it is below the maximum: k<4. B1

  9. Solve x−6x+8=0.

    Show answer

    Let u=x: u2−6u+8=0⇒(u−2)(u−4)=0⇒u=2 or 4. So x=4 or x=16.

Quick check
Summary
  • A quadratic has the form ax2+bx+c with a≠0. Its graph is a parabola: ∪-shaped if a>0, ∩-shaped if a<0.
  • Three ways to solve ax2+bx+c=0: factorising (fastest when it works), completing the square (also gives the vertex), and the formula x=−b±b2−4ac2a (always works).
  • In completed square form a(x+p)2+q, the vertex is (−p,q).
  • The discriminant b2−4ac gives the number of real roots: positive means 2, zero means 1 repeated root, negative means none.
  • For a line and a curve: set them equal, form a quadratic, and use the discriminant (2 points, tangent, or no meeting).
  • For inequalities: find critical values, sketch, then read the region from the graph.
  • Substitute a new letter for disguised quadratics such as x4−5x2+4=0.

Mathematics/Pure Mathematics 1

Functions

AS LevelExamsCAIE P1 · Edexcel IAL P1/P2 · UK Pure Years 1–2Study time6–8 hours

A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output. You will learn domain and range, one-one and many-one functions, composite and inverse functions, how restricting a domain makes an inverse possible, and how changes to an equation move, stretch and reflect a graph.

Why this matters

Every formula in science and business is a function: put in a time, get out a distance; put in a price, get out a profit. The language of functions (input, output, domain, range, inverse) lets you say exactly what a formula can and cannot do. It also gives you graph transformations, which let you sketch new curves from ones you already know, and it is the language that calculus is written in. Paper 1 regularly includes a multi-part functions question that combines a completed square, a range, an inverse and a composite function.

Before you start, you should be comfortable with Quadratics, especially completing the square, and with graphs from Coordinates and straight lines.

What is a function?

A function is a machine. You feed in a number, the machine follows a fixed rule, and out comes a new number. The square-root button on a calculator is a function: feed in 25 and you always get 5, never two different answers. That “one answer only” property is the heart of the definition.

Function

A rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input.

There are two ways to write the same function. Both of these mean “double the input, then add 3”:

f(x)=2x+3orf:x↦2x+3

Read f(4) as “f of 4”. It is the output when the input is 4, so f(4)=2(4)+3=11. The second form reads “f maps x to 2x+3”. Cambridge uses both forms.

Domain

The set of all allowed input values of a function.

Range

The set of all output values that the function actually produces.

The symbol ℝ stands for the real numbers (every number on the number line), and x∈ℝ means “x is any real number”. If a question gives no domain, use the largest set of real numbers for which the rule works. At this level only two things stop a rule working: dividing by zero and taking the square root of a negative number.

Function Largest domain Reason
1x−3 x≠3 cannot divide by 0
x−2 x≥2 cannot take the root of a negative
1x−2 x>2 the root must be positive, because it is also a denominator

To find the range, ask “which y-values does the graph reach?” A sketch or a completed square usually answers it.

TipWrite the range with f(x) or y

Write f(x)≥−3 or y≥−3. Never write x≥−3: x is the input, and the range is about outputs.

Worked exampleA function is defined by f(x)=x2−4x+1 for 0≤x≤5. Find the range of f.

Complete the square: f(x)=(x−2)2−3. The graph is ∪-shaped with its lowest point at x=2, which lies inside the domain, so the least value is −3.

Now check both ends of the domain: f(0)=1 and f(5)=25−20+1=6. The graph falls from 1 to −3, then rises to 6, so the greatest value is the larger end value, 6.

The range is −3≤f(x)≤6.

Common error: writing 1≤f(x)≤6 from the end values alone. That misses the dip to −3 at the vertex.

One-one and many-one functions

Compare f(x)=x3 and g(x)=x2. Every output of x3 comes from one input only. But g(2)=4 and g(−2)=4: two different inputs give the same output.

One-one function

A function in which each output comes from exactly one input.

Many-one function

A function in which at least one output comes from two or more different inputs.

The horizontal line test tells you which kind you have. Draw horizontal lines across the graph. If any line cuts the graph more than once, the function is many-one. If every line cuts it at most once, it is one-one.

A mapping where one input gives two outputs (such as y=±x) is not a function at all. This matters because only one-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

Sometimes you run one machine and feed its output into a second. The result is a composite function. Write fg(x) for f(g(x)): apply g first, then f. Work from the right.

Worked examplef(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x2−3, for x∈ℝ. Find fg(x) and gf(x), and solve gf(x)=6.

Start with fg(x): put g(x) into f. fg(x)=f(g(x))=f(x2−3)=2(x2−3)+1=2x2−5 Now gf(x): put f(x) into g. gf(x)=g(f(x))=g(2x+1)=(2x+1)2−3=4x2+4x−2 The two answers differ, so order matters.

To solve gf(x)=6: 4x2+4x−2=64x2+4x−8=0x2+x−2=0(x+2)(x−1)=0 Hence x=−2 or x=1.

Check: f(1)=3 and g(3)=9−3=6. It works.

Writing f2(x) means ff(x), “do f twice”. For fg to exist, every output of g must be an allowed input for f. With f(x)=x and g(x)=x−5 for x≥5, the outputs of g are all at least 0, so fg(x)=x−5 is fine. If g were defined for all real x, some outputs would be negative and fg would break down.

Common mistakeRead composites from the right

fg(x) is not “f times g”, and it does not mean “f first”. It means f(g(x)), so g acts first. Mixing up fg and gf is a very common way to lose marks.

Inverse functions

An inverse function undoes what the original did. If f turns 3 into 7, then f−1 turns 7 back into 3. A kettle that heats water is undone by letting it cool; subtracting 5 undoes adding 5.

Inverse function

For a one-one function f, the inverse function f−1 reverses f: if f(a)=b then f−1(b)=a. The domain of f−1 is the range of f, and the range of f−1 is the domain of f.

So f−1f(x)=x and ff−1(x)=x. To find an inverse:

  1. Write y=f(x).
  2. Rearrange to make x the subject.
  3. Replace y by x in your answer, and write it as f−1(x).
  4. State the domain of f−1: it is the range of f.
Worked examplef(x)=2x+1x−3 for x≠3. Find f−1(x), and state its domain.

Write y=2x+1x−3 and clear the fraction. Then collect the x terms on one side and factorise: y(x−3)=2x+1xy−3y=2x+1xy−2x=3y+1x(y−2)=3y+1x=3y+1y−2 So f−1(x)=3x+1x−2.

For the domain, find the range of f. Since 2x+1=2(x−3)+7, we can write f(x)=2+7x−3. The fraction is never zero, so f(x) never equals 2. The range is f(x)≠2, so the domain of f−1 is x≠2. This matches the denominator of f−1(x).

Check: f(4)=9 and f−1(9)=287=4. We return to the start.

Common mistakef⁻¹ is not 1/f

The “−1” in f−1(x) labels the inverse function. It does not mean 1f(x). For f(x)=2x, the inverse is f−1(x)=x2, while 1f(x)=12x.

The graph of an inverse

Because f takes a to b and f−1 takes b back to a, every point (a,b) on the graph of f matches a point (b,a) on the graph of f−1. Swapping coordinates is a reflection in the line y=x. Domain and range swap as well.

If a question asks you to solve f(x)=f−1(x) and f is an increasing function, the two graphs meet on the line y=x, so it is enough to solve f(x)=x.

Restricting a domain

The function f(x)=x2−4x+7 for x∈ℝ is many-one: the parabola is symmetrical, so two inputs share each output. But we are free to choose the domain. If we cut the parabola in half at its line of symmetry, each half is one-one and has an inverse. The line of symmetry comes from the completed square:

f(x)=(x−2)2+3

The vertex is (2,3). Restricting to x≥2 keeps the right-hand half, whose range is f(x)≥3. To find the inverse, rearrange y=(x−2)2+3 to get (x−2)2=y−3, so x−2=±y−3. Which sign? The original domain is x≥2, so x−2 is positive and we take the plus sign:

f−1(x)=2+x−3,x≥3

Had the domain been x≤2, we would take the minus sign, giving f−1(x)=2−x−3.

Exam techniqueDomains in inverse questions

“Find the smallest value of k for which f is one-one when x≥k” asks for the x-coordinate of the vertex. Marks for “state the domain of f−1” are easy to lose: it is always the range of f, written with x, for example x≥3.

Worked example(Exam style) The function f is defined by f(x)=3x2−12x+5 for x≥k. (a) Express f(x) in the form a(x−p)2+q. (b) State the smallest value of k for which f is one-one. (c) For this value of k, find f−1(x) and state its domain.

(a) Take out a factor of 3 from the first two terms, then complete the square inside: 3x2−12x+5=3(x2−4x)+5=3[(x−2)2−4]+5 M1 =3(x−2)2−7 A1

(b) The line of symmetry is x=2, so the smallest value is k=2. B1

(c) Let y=3(x−2)2−7. Then y+73=(x−2)2. M1

Because x≥2, take the positive root: x=2+y+73, so f−1(x)=2+x+73 A1

The domain of f−1 is the range of f. The least value of f is −7, so the domain is x≥−7. B1

Transformations of graphs

If you know the graph of y=f(x), you can sketch many related graphs without plotting points. Each change to the equation moves, stretches or reflects the picture in a predictable way.

Equation Transformation of y=f(x)
y=f(x)+a translation (0a): up a
(x,y)→(x, y+a)
y=f(x+a) translation (−a0): left a
(x,y)→(x−a, y)
y=af(x) stretch parallel to the y-axis, scale factor a
(x,y)→(x, ay)
y=f(ax) stretch parallel to the x-axis, scale factor 1a
(x,y)→(xa, y)
y=−f(x) reflection in the x-axis
(x,y)→(x, −y)
y=f(−x) reflection in the y-axis
(x,y)→(−x, y)

Why does f(x+2) move the graph left? Suppose f(3)=5, so (3,5) lies on y=f(x). On the new graph, the input that gives output 5 is the one with x+2=3, that is x=1. The point has moved from (3,5) to (1,5), two units to the left. The same reasoning shows that f(2x) reaches every output when x is only half as big, so the graph is squashed towards the y-axis.

Key factsThe inside/outside rule

Changes outside the bracket act on y and do what you expect: +a lifts, ×a stretches vertically. Changes inside the bracket act on x and do the opposite: x+a moves left, ax squashes horizontally by 1a.

Try the sliders. The first curve is y=x2 and the second is the transformed copy. Move c and d to slide the copy sideways and up or down. Move a to stretch it, and push a below zero to flip it over.

When transformations are combined, work in the order you would calculate. For y=3f(x)+1, start with f(x), multiply by 3, then add 1: stretch first, then translate. For a bracket such as f(2x−4), first factorise it as f(2(x−2)). Then squash by 12 parallel to the x-axis, and translate 2 to the right.

Common mistakeOrder matters

3f(x)+1 and 3(f(x)+1)=3f(x)+3 are different graphs. Always stretch before you translate vertically. A full description of a transformation needs its type and its details: a translation needs a vector, a stretch needs a direction and a scale factor, and a reflection needs a line.

Worked example(Exam style) The curve y=f(x) has a minimum point at (2,−3). Write down the coordinates of the minimum point on each curve: (a) y=f(x+1)−4, (b) y=2f(x), (c) y=f(3x), (d) y=−f(x). (e) Describe fully the two transformations that map y=f(x) onto y=3f(x−2)+1, and give the image of the minimum point.

(a) Left 1 and down 4: (2−1,  −3−4)=(1,−7). B1

(b) The y-coordinate doubles: (2,−6). B1

(c) The x-coordinate is divided by 3: (23,−3). B1

(d) The graph is reflected in the x-axis: (2,3), and it is now a maximum point. B1

(e) A stretch parallel to the y-axis with scale factor 3, B1 followed by a translation of (21). B1

The minimum point moves (2,−3)→(2,−9)→(4,−8). B1

Board differences

Cambridge puts all of this in Paper 1 (AS). The UK boards (AQA, OCR, Pearson Edexcel) split it: graph transformations are in Year 1, but domain and range, composite and inverse functions, and modulus functions are A Level (Year 2) content. Edexcel IAL covers the same ideas across P1 and P2. Notation differs slightly: Cambridge often writes f:x↦2x+3, the UK boards usually write f(x)=2x+3, and every board accepts both. Modulus functions such as y=∣f(x)∣ are in Cambridge Paper 3; see Algebra: modulus, polynomials and partial fractions.

Try it yourselfStart easy, finish at exam standard

  1. Let f(x)=3x−5. Find f(4), f(−2) and the value of x for which f(x)=10.

    Show answer

    f(4)=12−5=7 and f(−2)=−6−5=−11. Solving 3x−5=10 gives 3x=15, so x=5.

  2. The function g is defined by g(x)=2x2−8x+3 for x≥3. Find the range of g.

    Show answer

    Complete the square: g(x)=2(x−2)2−5, with its vertex at x=2. That is not in the domain x≥3. For x≥3 the graph only rises, so the least value is g(3)=18−24+3=−3. The range is g(x)≥−3.

  3. f(x)=x+4 and g(x)=3x2 for x∈ℝ. Find fg(x) and gf(x), and solve fg(x)=gf(x).

    Show answer

    fg(x)=3x2+4 and gf(x)=3(x+4)2=3x2+24x+48. Setting them equal, the 3x2 terms cancel: 4=24x+48, so 24x=−44 and x=−116.

  4. Find the inverse of f(x)=5x−2 for x≠2, and state the domain of f−1.

    Show answer

    Let y=5x−2. Then x−2=5y, so x=2+5y and f−1(x)=2+5x. The fraction 5x−2 is never zero, so the range of f is f(x)≠0. The domain of f−1 is therefore x≠0.

  5. f(x)=x2−6x+10 for x≥k. (a) Write f(x) in completed square form. (b) State the smallest k for which f is one-one. (c) For this k, find f−1(x) and its domain.

    Show answer

    (a) f(x)=(x−3)2+1. (b) The vertex is at x=3, so k=3. (c) y−1=(x−3)2, and since x≥3 we take the positive root: f−1(x)=3+x−1. The range of f is f(x)≥1, so the domain of f−1 is x≥1.

  6. State the single transformation that maps y=f(x) onto (a) y=f(x−3), (b) y=2f(x), (c) y=f ⁣(12x), (d) y=f(−x).

    Show answer

    (a) A translation of (30), that is 3 units to the right. (b) A stretch parallel to the y-axis with scale factor 2. (c) A stretch parallel to the x-axis with scale factor 2, because the scale factor is 1÷12. (d) A reflection in the y-axis.

  7. (Exam style) (a) Express x2−6x+4 in the form (x−p)2+q. (b) Describe the translation that maps the curve y=x2 onto the curve y=x2−6x+4. (c) Write down the equation of the line of symmetry of y=x2−6x+4.

    Show answer

    (a) Half of −6 is −3, so x2−6x=(x−3)2−9 and x2−6x+4=(x−3)2−5. [M1 A1] (b) Comparing with y=f(x−3)−5 where f(x)=x2: a translation of (3−5), that is 3 right and 5 down. B1 (c) The vertex is at (3,−5), so the line of symmetry is x=3. B1

  8. (Exam style) f(x)=3x−2 and g(x)=x2+1 for x∈ℝ. (a) Find gf(x). (b) Solve gf(x)=10. (c) Find f−1(x) and solve f(x)=f−1(x).

    Show answer

    (a) gf(x)=(3x−2)2+1=9x2−12x+5. [M1 A1] (b) (3x−2)2+1=10, so (3x−2)2=9 and 3x−2=±3. Hence x=53 or x=−13. [M1 A1] (c) From y=3x−2 we get x=y+23, so f−1(x)=x+23. B1 Solving 3x−2=x+23: 9x−6=x+2, so 8x=8 and x=1. [M1 A1] (Because f is increasing, solving f(x)=x gives the same answer: 3x−2=x, x=1.)

Quick check
Summary
  • A function gives exactly one output for each input. The domain is the set of allowed inputs and the range is the set of outputs produced. Write the range with f(x) or y.
  • A function is one-one if each output comes from one input (horizontal line test). Only one-one functions have inverses.
  • fg(x)=f(g(x)): apply g first. In general fg≠gf.
  • To find f−1: write y=f(x), make x the subject, then swap letters. Its domain is the range of f, and its graph is the reflection of f in y=x.
  • To make a quadratic one-one, restrict its domain to one side of the vertex, which you find by completing the square. Choose the ± in the inverse to match the original domain.
  • Outside the bracket, f(x)+a and af(x) act on y as expected. Inside, f(x+a) moves left by a and f(ax) stretches horizontally by 1a. −f(x) reflects in the x-axis and f(−x) in the y-axis.
  • For combined transformations, work in the order you would calculate: stretch first, then translate.

Next: Coordinate geometry uses equations to describe straight lines and circles, and you will meet transformed circles again there.

Mathematics/Probability and Statistics

The Poisson distribution

A Level (A2)ExamsCAIE P6 (S2) · Edexcel IAL S2 · UK Further Maths StatisticsStudy time5–7 hours

The Poisson distribution models the number of random events in a fixed interval of time or space, such as calls per hour or flaws per metre. You will learn its conditions, formula, mean and variance, how to rescale it, and how it approximates the binomial and is approximated by the normal distribution.

Why this matters

How many calls will a rescue centre receive between 2 am and 3 am? How many flaws will a 50 m cable have? How many goals will a team score? Each of these is a count of events that happen at random but with a steady average rate. Staffing, spare parts and guarantees all depend on knowing how likely each count is. The Poisson distribution is the standard model for this kind of problem, and it is one of the main ideas in Cambridge Paper 6.

Before you start, you should know the binomial distribution from Discrete random variables and the normal distribution from The normal distribution. You will also use the number e≈2.718 from Logarithms and exponentials.

Counting random events

The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of trials, so its count can never exceed n. Many real counts have no trials and no upper limit: emails arriving in an hour, typing errors on a page, atoms decaying in a second. The count could be 0,1,2,3,… and, in principle, anything larger. The Poisson distribution models counts like these.

Poisson distribution

The distribution of a random variable X that counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when the events occur singly, at random, independently of each other and at a constant average rate. We write X∼Po(λ), where λ is the mean number of events in the interval.

The three conditions need a closer look, because exam questions ask you to state them and to say when they fail.

  1. Singly. Two events cannot happen at exactly the same moment or place. Cars that arrive in convoys break this rule.
  2. Independently and at random. One event does not make another more or less likely. Road accidents in fog often fail this, because one crash causes the next.
  3. Constant average rate. The mean number of events is the same for every interval of the same size. Calls to a pizza shop fail this, because Friday evening is far busier than Monday afternoon.
Exam techniqueConditions in context

“State a condition for a Poisson model” wants the condition written in the context of the question, for example “the calls arrive independently of each other”. A bare “it is random” is too vague. For “explain why the model may not be suitable”, say which condition fails and why.

The formula, the mean and the variance

Key factsThe Poisson distribution

If X∼Po(λ), then P(X=r)=e−λ λrr!,r=0,1,2,3,… E(X)=λandVar(X)=λ

Here r! means r×(r−1)×⋯×1, and 0!=1. The probability of no events is P(X=0)=e−λ. All the probabilities add to 1 because 1+λ+λ22!+⋯=eλ.

The mean and the variance are equal. That is unusual and useful: if data have a mean and a variance that are very different, a Poisson model is doubtful.

TipBuilding probabilities step by step

Each probability comes from the one before: P(X=r+1)=λr+1 P(X=r). For λ=4: P(0)=e−4=0.0183, then P(1)=4×0.0183=0.0733, then P(2)=42×0.0733=0.1465. Keep full calculator accuracy and round only at the end.

Poisson counts have no upper limit, so “at least” and “more than” need the complement.

Words in the question Meaning Calculate
at most 3, no more than 3 X≤3 P(0)+P(1)+P(2)+P(3)
fewer than 3 X≤2 P(0)+P(1)+P(2)
at least 3 X≥3 1−P(X≤2)
more than 3 X≥4 1−P(X≤3)
Worked exampleEmails arrive at random, with a mean of 4 per hour. Find the probability that in a given hour (a) exactly 3 arrive, (b) at most 2 arrive, (c) at least 6 arrive.

Let X be the number of emails in an hour. Then X∼Po(4).

(a) P(X=3)=e−4 433!=323e−4=0.195

(b) P(X≤2)=e−4(1+4+422)=13e−4=0.238

(c) “At least 6” is the opposite of “at most 5”, so P(X≥6)=1−e−4(1+4+8+323+323+12815)=1−0.7851=0.215

Changing the interval

The mean λ belongs to one particular interval. Because the rate is constant, a longer or shorter interval has a proportionally larger or smaller mean.

Key factsScaling the mean

If events occur at a constant average rate of k per unit of time (or length, or area), the number of events in an interval of size t has distribution Po(kt).

Always write down the new distribution before you calculate. Counts in separate intervals add, and so do their means: if the number of emails in one hour is Po(4), the number in two hours is Po(8). Linear combinations of random variables proves this.

Common mistakeScale the mean, not the probability

If P(no flaws in 10 m)=0.449, then P(no flaws in 20 m) is not 2×0.449. Double the mean to λ=1.6 and recalculate: e−1.6=0.202. As a check, both 10 m halves must be flawless, and 0.4492=0.202.

Worked exampleFlaws occur at random in a cable at an average rate of 0.8 per 10 m. Find the probability that (a) a 25 m length has no flaws, (b) a 5 m length has at least 2 flaws.

(a) In 25 m the mean is 0.8×2.5=2.0, so X∼Po(2) and P(X=0)=e−2=0.135 (b) In 5 m the mean is 0.8×0.5=0.4, so Y∼Po(0.4) and P(Y≥2)=1−P(Y=0)−P(Y=1)=1−e−0.4(1+0.4)=1−0.9384=0.0616

Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

A binomial B(n,p) with large n and small p counts rare events among many trials, which is the Poisson situation. Its mean is np and its variance is npq. When p is small, q=1−p is close to 1, so the variance is close to the mean, just as for a Poisson variable. That is why Po(np) fits.

Binomial B(n,p) Poisson Po(λ)
What is counted successes in n trials events in an interval
Possible values 0,1,…,n 0,1,2,… with no limit
Mean and variance np and npq both equal to λ
Parameters two: n and p one: λ
Key factsPoisson approximation to the binomial

If X∼B(n,p) with n>50 and np<5, then X is approximately Po(np).

Worked exampleIn a factory 2% of light bulbs are faulty, independently of each other. A random sample of 150 bulbs is tested. (a) Explain why a Poisson distribution is a suitable approximation. (b) Use it to find the probability that at most 2 bulbs are faulty. (c) Find the exact probability and comment.

(a) Let X be the number of faulty bulbs, so X∼B(150,0.02). Here n=150>50 and np=3<5. B1 So X is approximately Po(3). B1

(b) P(X≤2)≈e−3(1+3+92)=8.5e−3 M1 =0.423 A1

(c) Exactly, P(X≤2)=0.98150+150(0.02)(0.98)149+(1502)(0.02)2(0.98)148=0.421. B1 The two answers differ by only 0.002, so the approximation is very good. B1

The normal approximation to the Poisson

Look again at the third panel of the figure. When λ is large the Poisson distribution is nearly symmetric and bell-shaped, so a normal curve with the same mean and variance fits it.

Key factsNormal approximation to the Poisson

If X∼Po(λ) with λ>15, then X is approximately N(λ,λ). The mean is λ, the variance is λ and the standard deviation is λ.

A Poisson variable takes whole numbers only, while a normal variable is continuous. In the figure below, the bar for r=20 is centred on 20 and stretches from 19.5 to 20.5. To include the whole bar we start the normal area at 19.5. This adjustment is called the continuity correction.

Continuity correction

The adjustment of 0.5 made when a discrete variable (taking whole numbers) is approximated by a continuous one, so that each whole number is represented by the interval from 0.5 below to 0.5 above it.

Let Y be the normal variable.

Poisson probability Normal calculation
P(X=20) P(19.5<Y<20.5)
P(X≤20) P(Y<20.5)
P(X<20) P(Y<19.5)
P(X≥20) P(Y>19.5)
P(X>20) P(Y>20.5)
TipA reliable routine

First rewrite the inequality so it contains “≤” or “≥” and a whole number (so X<20 becomes X≤19). Then add 0.5 to a “≤” value and subtract 0.5 from a “≥” value. A quick sketch of the bars confirms the choice.

Worked exampleX∼Po(24). Use a normal approximation to find P(X≥30).

Since λ=24>15, use Y∼N(24,24), so σ=24=4.899.

P(X≥30)≈P(Y>29.5) Standardise: z=29.5−2424=1.123, so P(Y>29.5)=1−Φ(1.123)=0.131 The exact Poisson answer is 0.132, so the approximation is good.

Common mistakeVariance, not standard deviation

For N(λ,λ) the second number is the variance. Divide by λ, not by λ, when you standardise. Forgetting the continuity correction costs a mark in every exam question on this topic.

Worked exampleCars pass a speed camera at random, at a constant average rate of 3.2 per minute. (a) State two conditions needed for a Poisson model. (b) Find the probability that exactly 2 cars pass in a given minute. (c) Find the probability that fewer than 3 cars pass in a 30-second period. (d) Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that more than 20 cars pass in a 5-minute period.

(a) Cars pass singly (never two at exactly the same instant) and independently of each other. [B1 B1]

(b) X∼Po(3.2), so P(X=2)=e−3.2 3.222!=0.209. [M1 A1]

(c) In 30 seconds the mean is 1.6, so Y∼Po(1.6). B1 P(Y<3)=P(Y≤2)=e−1.6(1+1.6+1.622)=0.783 [M1 A1]

(d) In 5 minutes the mean is 16, so W∼Po(16). Since 16>15, W is approximately N(16,16). B1 “More than 20” means W≥21, so P(W>20)≈P(N>20.5). M1 z=20.5−1616=1.125,1−Φ(1.125)=0.130 [M1 A1]

Board differences

Cambridge 9709 examines the Poisson distribution only in Paper 6 (Probability and Statistics 2) and states the conditions n>50, np<5 and λ>15. Edexcel IAL covers it in Statistics 2 with the same two approximations, but describes the conditions loosely (“n large, p small”, “λ large”), so follow the wording of the question. AQA, OCR and Edexcel A Level Mathematics in the UK do not include the Poisson distribution; it appears in their A Level Further Mathematics statistics options.

Try it yourselfStart easy, finish at exam standard

  1. X∼Po(1.5). Find (a) P(X=2), (b) P(X≥1).

    Show answer

    (a) P(X=2)=e−1.5×1.522=0.251. (b) P(X≥1)=1−P(X=0)=1−e−1.5=0.777.

  2. Say whether a Poisson model is reasonable in each case. If not, state which condition fails or why the variable is not Poisson. (a) The number of texts you receive in each hour of a whole day. (b) The number of sixes in 12 rolls of a die. (c) The number of accidents per day on a motorway, when one crash in fog is usually followed by several more.

    Show answer

    (a) Not reasonable: the rate is not constant (many more texts in the evening than at 4 am), and conversations make texts dependent. (b) Not Poisson: there are a fixed number of trials (12), so the count cannot exceed 12. It is binomial, B(12,16). (c) Not reasonable: accidents are not independent, because one crash makes another more likely.

  3. Typing errors occur at random, at a mean rate of 2 per page. Find the probability of (a) no errors on one page, (b) at least one error in 3 pages, (c) exactly 4 errors in 2 pages.

    Show answer

    (a) X∼Po(2): P(X=0)=e−2=0.135. (b) In 3 pages the mean is 6: P(Y≥1)=1−e−6=0.998. (c) In 2 pages the mean is 4: P(W=4)=e−4 444!=0.195.

  4. X∼Po(λ) and P(X=0)=0.2. Find λ and hence P(X=1).

    Show answer

    e−λ=0.2, so λ=ln⁡5=1.609. Then P(X=1)=λe−λ=1.609×0.2=0.322.

  5. Y∼Po(λ) and P(Y=3)=2P(Y=2). Find λ and P(Y≤4).

    Show answer

    P(Y=3)P(Y=2)=λ3, so λ3=2 and λ=6. [M1 A1] P(Y≤4)=e−6(1+6+18+36+54)=115e−6=0.285. [M1 A1]

  6. X∼B(80,0.03). Show that a Poisson approximation is suitable and use it to find P(X≥3).

    Show answer

    n=80>50 and np=2.4<5, so X is approximately Po(2.4). P(X≥3)=1−e−2.4(1+2.4+2.422)=1−0.5697=0.430.

  7. X∼Po(20). Use a normal approximation to find P(X<15).

    Show answer

    X is approximately Y∼N(20,20). P(X<15)=P(X≤14)≈P(Y<14.5). M1 z=14.5−2020=−1.230, so the probability is Φ(−1.230)=0.109. [M1 A1]

  8. (Exam style) A bakery sells a speciality loaf at random, at a mean rate of 4 loaves per day. (a) The bakery bakes 7 loaves each day. Find the probability that it runs out, meaning demand is more than 7. (b) The bakery wants the probability of running out to be less than 1%. What is the smallest number of loaves it should bake each day? (c) Baking 7 loaves a day, find the probability that it runs out on exactly 2 of the next 5 days.

    Show answer

    (a) X∼Po(4). P(X>7)=1−P(X≤7)=1−0.9489=0.0511. [M1 A1] (b) We need P(X>n)<0.01, that is P(X≤n)>0.99. M1 P(X≤8)=0.9786, which is too small, but P(X≤9)=0.9919. The bakery should bake 9 loaves. A1 (c) The days are independent, so the number of run-out days is B(5,0.0511). M1 P(exactly 2)=(52)(0.0511)2(0.9489)3=0.0223. A1

Quick checkQuick check
Summary
  • A Poisson variable counts events in a fixed interval when events occur singly, independently and at a constant average rate. Write X∼Po(λ).
  • P(X=r)=e−λλrr! for r=0,1,2,…, with E(X)=Var(X)=λ.
  • “At least” and “more than” use the complement: P(X≥3)=1−P(X≤2).
  • Scale the mean, never the probability: rate k per unit gives Po(kt) over an interval of size t.
  • If X∼B(n,p) with n>50 and np<5, then X≈Po(np).
  • If X∼Po(λ) with λ>15, then X≈N(λ,λ). Use the continuity correction of 0.5.
  • In exam answers, state conditions in context and show the substituted formula before the calculator value.

Next: Linear combinations of random variables shows how to add independent random variables, including Poisson ones.

PreviousFunctionsNextForces and equilibrium
Mathematics/Mechanics

Forces and equilibrium

AS LevelExamsCAIE P4 · Edexcel IAL M1 · UK MechanicsStudy time5–7 hours

Mechanics begins with forces. You will learn to name the forces on an object, draw a force diagram, resolve forces into components, find a resultant, and use equilibrium, friction and Newton’s third law on flat surfaces and slopes.

Why this matters

Every bridge, crane, climbing rope and roof is designed so that the forces on it balance. If they do not, something moves, usually in the wrong direction. Mechanics is the mathematics of forces and motion. It is a short, high-scoring paper (Cambridge Paper 4) once you can draw a good force diagram, and this chapter teaches the skills that every later mechanics chapter uses: spotting forces, splitting them into components and writing equations.

Before you start, you need right-angled triangle trigonometry from Geometry and basic trigonometry and confident algebra from Algebra from scratch. Slopes use sin⁡ and cos⁡ of angles, as in Trigonometry.

Forces and the mechanics model

A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons (N). They have both a size and a direction, so they are vectors: a force of 10 N means nothing until you say which way it acts.

Force

A push or a pull on an object. It is a vector quantity, measured in newtons (N). A resultant force on an object changes its velocity.

Resultant force

The single force that has the same effect as all the forces on an object together. It is the vector sum of the forces.

Real objects are complicated, so mechanics replaces them with simple models. The words in an exam question tell you what to ignore.

Word in the question What it means for your model
particle All the mass is at one point. Ignore size, shape and spin.
light (string, rod, pulley) The mass is zero. A light string has the same tension at both ends.
inextensible string It does not stretch, so connected objects move together.
smooth No friction. The contact force is perpendicular to the surface.
rough Friction may act.
uniform (rod, plank) The mass is spread evenly, so the weight acts at the midpoint.
smooth pulley or peg A string slides over it freely, so the tension is the same on both sides.

The forces you will meet

Force Usual symbol Direction Where it comes from
Weight W=mg Vertically down Gravity pulling on mass m
Normal reaction R Perpendicular to the surface, away from it A surface pushing back
Friction F Along the surface, against sliding A rough surface
Tension T Along the string, pulling the object A taut string or rope
Thrust T Along a rod, pushing the object A compressed rod
Driving force D In the direction of motion An engine, or a person pushing
Resistance F or a number Against the motion Air, water, friction in the machinery

Mass m (in kg) measures how much matter an object has. Weight is the force of gravity on it, W=mg. Cambridge tells you to “take g=10”, so a 5 kg mass has weight 5×10=50 N. Edexcel and the UK boards use g=9.8, so the same mass weighs 49 N. Use whichever value the paper gives.

Normal reaction

The component of the contact force between two surfaces that acts at right angles (“normal”) to the surfaces, pushing the object away from the surface.

Force diagrams

A force diagram shows every force on one object. Nearly every mechanics mark depends on drawing it carefully, so do it first, every time.

  1. Draw the object as a box or a dot. For a particle, draw every force starting at the same point.
  2. Draw the weight W=mg straight down.
  3. Look at everything touching the object. For each surface draw a normal reaction R, and a friction force F if the surface is rough. For each string draw a tension T pulling away from the object along the string.
  4. Add any given forces (a push, a pull, a driving force) and any resistance.
  5. Label every force with its size or a letter, and mark the direction you will take as positive.
Common mistakeDo not invent forces

There is no “force of motion” and no “force of the throw” once a ball has left your hand. An object needs a force to change its velocity, not to keep moving. Every force on your diagram must come from something you can name: gravity, a surface, a string, an engine.

Resolving forces

A force at an angle can be replaced by two perpendicular forces, called its components, which together have exactly the same effect. Finding them is called resolving.

Key factsResolving a force

A force F at angle θ to a given direction has components

  • Fcos⁡θ along that direction, and
  • Fsin⁡θ perpendicular to it.

The angle must be measured from the direction you are resolving along. If you are given the angle to the other direction, swap cos⁡ and sin⁡.

Worked exampleA force of 20 N acts at 30∘ above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

Horizontal: 20cos⁡30∘=17.3 N.

Vertical: 20sin⁡30∘=10.0 N.

Check: 17.32+102=20, as it should be.

TipChoose your two directions wisely

You can resolve in any two perpendicular directions. Choose them so that as many unknown forces as possible lie along one of them. On a slope, resolve along and perpendicular to the slope. With strings, use horizontal and vertical.

Resultant of several forces

To find the resultant: choose x and y directions, add up all the x-components, add up all the y-components, then combine the two totals with Pythagoras and tan⁡.

Worked exampleTwo forces act on a particle at O. P=12 N acts along the positive x-axis. Q=10 N acts at 60∘ above the negative x-axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.

Components of Q: x-component −10cos⁡60∘=−5, and y-component 10sin⁡60∘=8.66.

Totals: X=12−5=7 N and Y=8.66 N.

magnitude=72+8.662=124=11.1 N tan⁡α=8.667⇒α=51.1∘

The resultant is 11.1 N, at 51.1∘ above the positive x-axis.

Equilibrium

Equilibrium

A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero. It is then either at rest or moving in a straight line at constant speed (Newton’s first law).

Equilibrium gives two equations, one for each of two perpendicular directions: the components in each direction add to zero. In words: forces up = forces down, and forces left = forces right.

Worked exampleA particle of mass 5 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light strings. One string makes 30∘ with the horizontal and the other makes 60∘ with the horizontal, on opposite sides. Find the tension in each string. Take g=10.

The weight is 5×10=50 N. Let T1 be the tension in the 30∘ string and T2 the tension in the 60∘ string.

Horizontally, left equals right: T1cos⁡30∘=T2cos⁡60∘⇒T2=3 T1 Vertically, up equals down: T1sin⁡30∘+T2sin⁡60∘=50 Substitute T2=3 T1: 12T1+3⋅32T1=12T1+32T1=2T1=50 So T1=25 N and T2=253=43.3 N.

Sense check: the steeper string carries more of the weight, so its tension is larger.

Friction

When two rough surfaces are pushed together, a friction force acts along the surfaces and resists sliding.

Friction

A contact force that acts along the surfaces, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). It is zero for a smooth contact.

Friction can only be as big as the situation needs, up to a maximum that depends on how hard the surfaces are pressed together:

Key factsThe friction law

F≤μR where R is the normal reaction and μ is the coefficient of friction between the two surfaces. When the object is about to slip (limiting equilibrium) or is sliding, F=μR, and friction acts against the motion (or the direction it would move).

Limiting friction

The maximum value of friction, μR, reached when an object is on the point of slipping.

The contact force between two surfaces is the resultant of R and F. Its magnitude is R2+F2.

Common mistakeFriction is not always μR

Take a 10 kg box on a floor with μ=0.4 (so R=100 N and the maximum friction is 40 N). If you push it with only 30 N, nothing moves, and the friction is 30 N, not 40 N. Friction matches the push until the push exceeds μR. Write F=μR only when the question says “limiting equilibrium”, “about to slip” or “sliding”.

Worked exampleA crate of mass 10 kg lies on rough horizontal ground with coefficient of friction 0.4. A rope at 30∘ above the horizontal pulls it. Find the tension in the rope when the crate is about to slide. Take g=10.

The rope lifts the crate slightly, so R is less than the weight.

Vertically: R+Tsin⁡30∘=100, so R=100−0.5T.

Horizontally: Tcos⁡30∘=F. The crate is about to slide, so F=0.4R. Tcos⁡30∘=0.4(100−0.5T)⇒T(cos⁡30∘+0.2)=40 T=401.0660=37.5 N Then R=100−0.5(37.5)=81.2 N.

Inclined planes

On a slope, resolve along the slope and perpendicular to it. Gravity does not point along either direction, so the weight must be split.

Key factsWeight on a slope inclined at angle θ
  • Component of weight down the slope: mgsin⁡θ
  • Component of weight into the slope: mgcos⁡θ
  • With no other forces perpendicular to the slope, R=mgcos⁡θ.
  • A block just about to slide down a rough slope, with no other forces, has μ=tan⁡θ.
Worked example(Exam style) A block of mass 5 kg rests on a rough plane inclined at angle θ to the horizontal, where sin⁡θ=0.6 and cos⁡θ=0.8. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is 0.5. A force of magnitude P N acts on the block up the plane, parallel to a line of greatest slope. Find the set of values of P for which the block stays in equilibrium. Take g=10.

Perpendicular to the plane: R=50cos⁡θ=50×0.8=40 N. [M1 A1]

Maximum friction: Fmax⁡=0.5×40=20 N. B1

The weight component down the plane is 50sin⁡θ=30 N. B1

Least P: the block is about to slide down, so friction acts up the plane. Resolving along the plane: P+20=30, so P=10. [M1 A1]

Greatest P: the block is about to slide up, so friction acts down the plane. Resolving along the plane: P=30+20=50. [M1 A1]

The block is in equilibrium for 10≤P≤50. A1

Newton’s third law

Newton’s third law

If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type of force and act on different objects.

Think of two ice-skaters who push off from each other: each feels the same size of force, in opposite directions. A common error concerns a book on a table. The weight of the book and the normal reaction on the book are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair, because both act on the book. The partner of the book’s weight is the book’s pull on the Earth. The partner of the table’s push on the book is the book’s push on the table.

In problems, the law tells you that a string pulling two particles has the same tension on both, and that two blocks in contact push on each other with equal and opposite forces.

Board differences

Cambridge 9709 Paper 4 and Edexcel IAL Mechanics 1 treat this topic in the same way and use the same model words. The differences are small. Cambridge says “take g=10” and expects 3 significant figures. Edexcel IAL and the UK boards use g=9.8 and expect 2 or 3 significant figures. Edexcel IAL also gives forces as vectors in 𝐢 and 𝐣 notation, such as (3𝐢−2𝐣) N, which you add component by component. In the UK A Level Mathematics specifications (Edexcel, AQA, OCR), friction and F≤μR are second-year content.

Exam techniqueForces questions: where the marks are

Draw the force diagram before writing any equation, and mark the positive direction. Examiners give a method mark for each correct resolving equation, so write one equation for each direction. Give the full working for R before using F=μR. State “limiting equilibrium” when you use F=μR, and give answers to 3 significant figures.

Try it yourselfStart easy, finish at exam standard

  1. A force of 50 N acts at 40∘ above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

    Show answer

    Horizontal: 50cos⁡40∘=38.3 N. Vertical: 50sin⁡40∘=32.1 N.

  2. A particle of mass 2.5 kg hangs at rest from a light vertical string. Find the tension. Take g=10.

    Show answer

    Equilibrium: the tension balances the weight, T=2.5×10=25 N.

  3. A box of mass 8 kg rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction 0.25. A horizontal force of 15 N is applied to the box. Take g=10. (a) Show that the box does not move. (b) Find the friction force. (c) Find the magnitude of the contact force between the box and the floor.

    Show answer

    (a) R=80 N, so the maximum friction is 0.25×80=20 N. The push of 15 N is less than 20 N, so the box does not move. (b) The box is in equilibrium, so F=15 N (not 20 N). (c) Contact force =R2+F2=802+152=81.4 N.

  4. A particle of mass 6 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30∘ to the horizontal. It is held by a light string parallel to the plane. Find the tension in the string and the normal reaction. Take g=10.

    Show answer

    Along the plane: T=60sin⁡30∘=30 N. Perpendicular to the plane: R=60cos⁡30∘=52.0 N.

  5. A block rests in limiting equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at 20∘ to the horizontal. No other force acts on it. Find the coefficient of friction.

    Show answer

    Along the plane: F=mgsin⁡20∘. Perpendicular: R=mgcos⁡20∘. Limiting: F=μR, so μ=tan⁡20∘=0.364.

  6. Forces of 6 N and 8 N act on a particle at right angles to each other. A third force F keeps the particle in equilibrium. Find the magnitude of F and the angle between F and the 8 N force.

    Show answer

    The resultant of the 6 N and 8 N forces is 36+64=10 N, at tan⁡−1(6/8)=36.9∘ to the 8 N force. F must be equal and opposite, so F=10 N, and the angle between F and the 8 N force is 180∘−36.9∘=143.1∘.

  7. (Exam style) A block of mass 4 kg is held in equilibrium on a smooth plane inclined at 30∘ to the horizontal by a horizontal force of magnitude P N. Find P and the normal reaction R. Take g=10.

    Show answer

    Resolve along the plane: Pcos⁡30∘=40sin⁡30∘. M1 P=40tan⁡30∘=23.1 N. A1 Resolve perpendicular to the plane: R=40cos⁡30∘+Psin⁡30∘. M1 R=34.64+11.55=46.2 N. A1

  8. (Exam style) A block of mass 3 kg is on a rough plane inclined at 30∘ to the horizontal, with coefficient of friction 0.2. A horizontal force P N pushes the block up the plane and the block is about to slide up. Find P. Take g=10.

    Show answer

    Perpendicular to the plane: R=30cos⁡30∘+Psin⁡30∘. [M1 A1] Along the plane (friction acts down the plane): Pcos⁡30∘=30sin⁡30∘+0.2R. [M1 A1] Substitute: Pcos⁡30∘=15+0.2(25.98+0.5P), so P(0.8660−0.1)=15+5.196. M1 P=20.1960.7660=26.4 N. A1

Quick check
Summary
  • A force is a vector, measured in newtons. Weight is W=mg; take g=10 (Cambridge) or g=9.8 (Edexcel and UK boards).
  • Always draw a force diagram: weight, then a normal reaction and friction at each surface, then tensions and any given forces.
  • A force F at angle θ to a direction has components Fcos⁡θ along it and Fsin⁡θ perpendicular to it.
  • The resultant comes from adding components in two perpendicular directions, then using Pythagoras and tan⁡.
  • Equilibrium means the resultant is zero: the components add to zero in each of two perpendicular directions.
  • Friction obeys F≤μR, with F=μR only when the object is about to slip or is sliding.
  • On a slope, the weight splits into mgsin⁡θ down the slope and mgcos⁡θ into it.
  • Newton’s third law: the two forces of a pair are equal, opposite, of the same type, and act on different objects.

TipHow to use quizzes well

Quizzes are retrieval practice: the act of pulling an answer out of memory is what makes it stick. Do a short quiz at the start of each study session on topics from last week, not just today’s topic.
